paragraphs.text: These short definitions support lookup after the explanations and examples in the main chapters.

[[**abducens nucleus:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A brainstem group containing the motor neurons recorded in the eye-drift study; their axons activate the lateral rectus eye muscle.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**activity bump:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A localized peak of population firing rates across neurons ordered by their preferred represented values.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**attractor manifold:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The continuous family of persistent activity states, described by its represented coordinates rather than by every neural activity separately.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Betti numbers:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Counts of independent connected components, loops, cavities, and their higher-dimensional counterparts.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Brownian motion:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A continuous random process starting at zero with independent Gaussian increments of mean zero and variance equal to elapsed time.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**causal filter:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A rule whose current output depends only on present and past input.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**coefficient of determination:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} For the optimal linear prediction with an intercept, the fraction of response variance removed by prediction; with one predictor it equals the squared correlation.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**coefficient of variation:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Standard deviation divided by mean; in the spike-train discussion it is applied to interspike intervals.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**continuous attractor:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and neutral motion along it in the ideal deterministic model.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**convolution:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An integral or sum combining past input values with a shifted response kernel to obtain a filtered output.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**correlation coefficient:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Covariance divided by the product of standard deviations; a dimensionless measure of linear association.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**covariance:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The mean product of two centered random variables, measuring their shared variation.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Cramér Rao bound:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A lower bound on local unbiased estimation variance under the required regularity conditions, expressed through inverse Fisher information.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**critical point:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A point where a function's gradient is zero. The Euler calculation also requires invertible Hessians.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**decoding:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Estimating a represented value from neural responses.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**dendrite:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A branching input structure of a neuron.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**diffusion coefficient:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The coefficient $D$ in the local one-dimensional displacement variance $2Dt$; its units are coordinate squared per time.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**diffusion tensor:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The matrix giving local coordinate-displacement covariances per twice the elapsed time.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Dirac delta:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A point-mass distribution; in the initial-condition equation all probability is concentrated at the specified coordinate.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**encoding:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Establishing a population activity pattern from an input.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Euler characteristic:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The alternating sum of Betti numbers; in three dimensions, components minus independent loops plus enclosed cavities.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**excess kurtosis:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The fourth centered moment divided by the squared variance, minus three. It is zero for a Gaussian population.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**excitatory input:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} In the models used here, an input that increases a receiving neuron's tendency to fire.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**excursion set:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The positions where a function exceeds a specified level.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**Fano factor:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Spike-count variance divided by mean count, for a specified counting interval and condition.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**firing rate:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The expected number of spikes per unit time, conditional on the modeled circumstances.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Fisher information:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The expected squared score, quantifying the local sensitivity of a probability distribution to a parameter.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**fixational drift:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Slow eye motion during attempted fixation, between rapid eye movements.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**fixed point:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A state whose deterministic rate of change is zero.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Fokker Planck equation:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An equation describing how a probability density evolves under drift and diffusion; the guide states the convention before using it.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**gain:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in another.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**gamma function:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The function $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du$ for $t>0$, extending factorials through $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**Gaussian curvature:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} For a surface in three dimensions, the product of its two principal curvatures.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Gaussian process:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A distribution over functions whose values at any finite collection of positions have a joint Gaussian distribution.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**grid cell:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A spatially tuned entorhinal neuron with repeated firing fields, often approximately hexagonally arranged in a two-dimensional arena.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**Hessian:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The matrix of second derivatives of a function with respect to its coordinates.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**hippocampus:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A brain region involved in memory and navigation.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**hyperbolic cotangent:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The function $\coth z=1/\tanh z$, for real $z\ne0$.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**hyperbolic tangent:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The function $\tanh z=(e^z-e^{-z})/(e^z+e^{-z})$.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**impulse response:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The output of a linear filter in response to a unit-area input impulse, from which responses to general input can be assembled.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**inhibitory input:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} In the models used here, an input that reduces a receiving neuron's tendency to fire.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**internal Fisher information rate:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The local information per unit observation time about the instantaneous attractor coordinate, as defined by the 2012 spike model.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**inverse hyperbolic tangent:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The inverse of $\tanh$ on $(-1,1)$, given by $\operatorname{artanh}z=\tfrac12\log[(1+z)/(1-z)]$.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**Isotropy:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Invariance of the spatial probability law under rotations.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Itô convention:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A stochastic-increment convention that evaluates the noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**jointly Gaussian vector:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A random vector for which every linear combination of its entries is Gaussian.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Kac–Rice formula:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A way to compute expected crossing or critical-point counts from the joint distribution of a random function and its derivatives, under the relevant regularity assumptions.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**left zero eigenvector:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A vector $v$ with $v^T A=0$; with appropriate normalization it extracts the persistent coordinate from a small state disturbance.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**likelihood:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The probability or density of the observed data considered as a function of a proposed parameter value.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**linearization:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The first-order approximation to a dynamical equation near a reference state.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**lognormal distribution:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A distribution of positive values whose logarithms are Gaussian.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**low pass filter:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A filter that suppresses sufficiently rapid input changes relative to slower ones.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**mean curvature:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} For a surface in three dimensions, the average of its two principal curvatures.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**mean squared displacement:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The average squared change in a coordinate across a specified time lag.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**microsaccades:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Brief, rapid eye movements that occur during attempted fixation.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Morse theory:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A theory relating the topology of a function's level-set regions to its critical points. The guide uses a signed critical-point count under its smoothness and nondegeneracy assumptions, including boundary contributions.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**neural transfer function:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The modeled relationship between a neuron's input and its expected firing rate.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**neuron:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A signaling cell in the nervous system.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**ocular motoneurons (OMNs):**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**ocular plant:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The muscles and mechanical eye system that transform motor activity into eye motion.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**oculomotor integrator:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A neural circuit that converts movement commands into a maintained eye-position command.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**p value:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Under the specified null comparison, the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme in the tested direction as the observed one.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**path integration:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Updating an estimate of position from movement.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**place cell:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A spatially selective hippocampal neuron that fires strongly in one or more localized regions of an environment.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**place field:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A connected region of elevated spatial firing, as defined by the model or stated measurement procedure.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Poisson process:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A counting process with independent increments and a deterministic constant or time-dependent event rate; its count over an interval has equal mean and variance. In a recurrent model, conditionally Poisson instantaneous spike generation does not make complete spike trains have independent increments.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**population code:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A representation carried by the pattern of responses across neurons.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**precision:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The reciprocal of variance for a scalar Gaussian estimate.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**preferred angle:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An angle where a neuron's tuning curve peaks.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**prior distribution:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A distribution representing knowledge about likely parameter values before observing the current data.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**rate map:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An estimate of spatial firing rate from spikes per time spent at each position.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Rayleigh distribution:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The distribution of a positive variable that is a scaled square root of an exponential variable.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**recurrent connectivity:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Connections that feed activity back into the same neuronal population.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**renewal process:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An event process with independent, identically distributed intervals under the fixed conditions being modeled.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**retina:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**right zero eigenvector:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A state-space direction $u$ satisfying $Au=0$ for the linearized dynamics.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**root mean squared displacement:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The square root of mean squared displacement, expressed in the original coordinate's units.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**score:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The derivative of log likelihood with respect to the parameter being estimated.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**skew:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The third centered moment divided by the variance to the power $3/2$, measuring asymmetry.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Smoothness:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The existence and regularity of derivatives of a function. The crossing and peak calculations require different derivative orders.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**spike:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A brief electrical event emitted by a neuron.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**standard error of the mean (SEM):**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An estimate of uncertainty in a sample mean. Its interpretation depends on which observations are treated as independent, such as trials, cells, or animals.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**state:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The quantities that specify a modeled system's current condition and determine its subsequent dynamics together with future inputs and noise.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**Stationarity:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} In the place-field model, invariance of spatial statistics under translating the map.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**stationary process:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A random process whose probability law is unchanged by shifting its time or position origin; weaker covariance-only stationarity must be specified when used.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**Stratonovich convention:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A stochastic-increment convention using midpoint evaluation in the limiting increments.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**sub-Poisson spiking:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Spiking with less variability than a matched Poisson reference according to the stated measure and conditions.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**superdiffusion:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Mean squared displacement growing faster than linearly with lag over the range being described.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**synapse:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A connection through which one neuron influences another.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**systematic drift:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A nonzero mean velocity of the represented coordinate, distinct from random spreading.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Translation invariance:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} In the readout model, invariance under shifts of the represented value. It makes the readout variance independent of the cue state.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**tuning curve:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A neuron's expected firing rate as a function of a represented variable.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**unbiased:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Describes an estimator whose expected value equals the parameter locally under the conditions used in the estimation bound.]{.definition-explanation}
[[**upcrossing:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A point where a function crosses upward through a specified threshold.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**weak fluctuation approximation:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An expansion about the deterministic population dynamics in which the aggregate effects of many small spike contributions remain small.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**Weibull distribution:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A positive-variable distribution with survival probability $\exp[-(s/b)^k]$, scale $b>0$, and shape $k>0$.]{.definition-explanation}

[[**White noise:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An ideal noise input with zero covariance at unequal times and a delta-function covariance at equal times; its integrated increments have finite variance.]{.definition-explanation}

"[[**root mean squared displacement:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The square root of mean squared displacement, expressed in the original coordinate's units.]{.definition-explanation}"
"[[**score:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The derivative of log likelihood with respect to the parameter being estimated.]{.definition-explanation}"
"[[**skew:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The third centered moment divided by the variance to the power $3/2$, measuring asymmetry.]{.definition-explanation}"
"The crossing and peak calculations require different derivative orders.]{.definition-explanation}"
"[[**Smoothness:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The existence and regularity of derivatives of a function."
"[[**spike:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A brief electrical event emitted by a neuron.]{.definition-explanation}"
"Its interpretation depends on which observations are treated as independent, such as trials, cells, or animals.]{.definition-explanation}"
"[[**standard error of the mean (SEM):**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An estimate of uncertainty in a sample mean."

"[[**state:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The quantities that specify a modeled system's current condition and determine its subsequent dynamics together with future inputs and noise.]{.definition-explanation}"
"[[**Stationarity:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} In the place-field model, invariance of spatial statistics under translating the map.]{.definition-explanation}"

"[[**stationary process:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A random process whose probability law is unchanged by shifting its time or position origin; weaker covariance-only stationarity must be specified when used.]{.definition-explanation}"
"[[**Stratonovich convention:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A stochastic-increment convention using midpoint evaluation in the limiting increments.]{.definition-explanation}"

"[[**sub-Poisson spiking:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Spiking with less variability than a matched Poisson reference according to the stated measure and conditions.]{.definition-explanation}"
"[[**superdiffusion:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Mean squared displacement growing faster than linearly with lag over the range being described.]{.definition-explanation}"
"[[**synapse:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A connection through which one neuron influences another.]{.definition-explanation}"
"[[**systematic drift:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A nonzero mean velocity of the represented coordinate, distinct from random spreading.]{.definition-explanation}"
"It makes the readout variance independent of the cue state.]{.definition-explanation}"
"[[**Translation invariance:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} In the readout model, invariance under shifts of the represented value."
"[[**tuning curve:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A neuron's expected firing rate as a function of a represented variable.]{.definition-explanation}"

"[[**unbiased:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Describes an estimator whose expected value equals the parameter locally under the conditions used in the estimation bound.]{.definition-explanation}"
"[[**upcrossing:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A point where a function crosses upward through a specified threshold.]{.definition-explanation}"

"[[**weak fluctuation approximation:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An expansion about the deterministic population dynamics in which the aggregate effects of many small spike contributions remain small.]{.definition-explanation}"

"[[**Weibull distribution:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A positive-variable distribution with survival probability $\exp[-(s/b)^k]$, scale $b>0$, and shape $k>0$.]{.definition-explanation}"

"[[**White noise:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An ideal noise input with zero covariance at unequal times and a delta-function covariance at equal times; its integrated increments have finite variance.]{.definition-explanation}"

"Its strongest tests ask whether fitting field sizes and counts also explains field shapes and holes.]{.key-statement}[^p3-question]"
"Once a map is drawn, it is fixed while the animal moves through it."

paragraphs.text: The study compares recordings of hippocampal place cells from bats flying through tunnels, rats moving over an arena floor, and bats flying through a room. For tunnel flights, the analysis uses distance along an approximately one-dimensional route, although the tunnel itself has width and height. The floor map uses two position coordinates, and the room map uses three.

A cell recorded on a short track may have one smooth firing hill. [On a long track, the same kind of cell may have several separated fields, each with a different width and height. In a room, its active regions can bend, split, and surround inactive holes. How could one model produce this variety and still make useful predictions?]{.key-statement}

Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak propose that a cell's spatial input is a smooth random function. This function can be interpreted as the average combined input arriving through the cell's synapses at each animal position. The model cell has positive firing rate where this input exceeds a threshold. The recordings estimate firing rates rather than measuring this input directly.[^p3-model] [The model predicts distributions of field lengths, areas, and volumes, rather than the location of a particular cell's next field. Its strongest tests ask whether fitting field sizes and counts also explains field shapes and holes.]{.key-statement}[^p3-question]

We begin on a track, where a field starts at [an [**upcrossing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a point where the input crosses upward through the threshold.]{.definition-explanation} Counting these crossings gives the average number of fields. Combining that count with the lengths of active fields and inactive gaps then separates the effect of the threshold from the distance over which the map changes. These calculations establish the parameters needed for the later predictions of sizes and shapes.

[Spatial randomness here describes different possible rate maps. Once a map is drawn, it is fixed while the animal moves through it. The spatial coordinate is not time, and the model does not by itself describe memory drift, spike timing, or learning.]{.key-statement}

review_metadata.title: Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale
review_metadata.purpose: Hippocampal place cells fire more at particular locations as an animal moves. This chapter introduces the rodent and bat recordings, then shows how a smooth random input that exceeds a firing threshold can produce several separate active regions for one cell.

section_list.title: Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fields
section_list.summary: To predict a field's width, we need to relate activity at nearby positions. A histogram of firing rates alone loses that information: rearranging its values could turn one broad field into many tiny fields without changing the histogram.

section_list.title: Upcrossings count fields, with an endpoint correction
section_list.summary: A field starts at an upcrossing, so its expected count can be found by counting upward passages through the threshold. A small interval around each crossing has a width determined by its slope; this lets us count crossings without locating every root.

section_list.title: Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scale
section_list.summary: A low field count can result from a high threshold or a slowly varying map. Field lengths help separate those possibilities.

blocks.caption: Two upcrossings start two new fields, and one field is already active at the left edge. The local tangent panels show that a steeper crossing occupies a narrower threshold band, while slope weighting makes each crossing contribute one. This is a guide construction, not a sampled cell or a new fit; it illustrates Mainali et al. (2025), Figure 1A–B and Supplemental Methods S3, Equations S11–S15.
blocks.alt: A constructed smooth curve crosses q upward twice and has three active intervals because the first begins before the left edge of the track. One full field and one gap are marked. Two local tangent plots use the same vertical band q plus or minus epsilon; the steeper slope has a narrower horizontal width 2 epsilon divided by v, and slope times width divided by 2 epsilon equals one in both cases.

blocks.caption: One fixed Gaussian input draw becomes a nonnegative firing map through $F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+$. Values below $q$ become zero; values above $q$ are reduced by $q$ and multiplied by $a$. The shaded connected intervals are the model fields. This is a simulated teaching map with chosen parameters, not a recorded cell. Based on Mainali et al. (2025), Fig. 1A and STAR Methods Eqs. 2–3, p. e1.
blocks.alt: The upper plot shows one fixed smooth input against spatial position, with a threshold at 0.8 and shaded intervals above it. The lower plot uses the same positions and plots six times the positive excess above the threshold in hertz. Its connected positive intervals align with the upper shading; all other positions have zero firing.

blocks.caption: A thresholded Gaussian map explains field lengths, gaps and higher moments in one dimensional recordings. Original Figure 1 from Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025); exact artwork excerpt. [PDF page 4](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=4). [Open image at full size](../assets/fig-paper-place-1.png).

# Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale {#ch:PLACE-FIELDS} The study compares recordings of hippocampal place cells from bats flying through tunnels, rats moving over an arena floor, and bats flying through a room. For tunnel flights, the analysis uses distance along an approximately one-dimensional route, although the tunnel itself has width and height. The floor map uses two position coordinates, and the room map uses three. A cell recorded on a short track may have one smooth firing hill. [On a long track, the same kind of cell may have several separated fields, each with a different width and height. In a room, its active regions can bend, split, and surround inactive holes. How could one model produce this variety and still make useful predictions?]{.key-statement} Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak propose that a cell's spatial input is a smooth random function. This function can be interpreted as the average combined input arriving through the cell's synapses at each animal position. The model cell has positive firing rate where this input exceeds a threshold. The recordings estimate firing rates rather than measuring this input directly.[^p3-model] [The model predicts distributions of field lengths, areas, and volumes, rather than the location of a particular cell's next field. Its strongest tests ask whether fitting field sizes and counts also explains field shapes and holes.]{.key-statement}[^p3-question] We begin on a track, where a field starts at [an [**upcrossing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a point where the input crosses upward through the threshold.]{.definition-explanation} Counting these crossings gives the average number of fields. Combining that count with the lengths of active fields and inactive gaps then separates the effect of the threshold from the distance over which the map changes. These calculations establish the parameters needed for the later predictions of sizes and shapes. [Spatial randomness here describes different possible rate maps. Once a map is drawn, it is fixed while the animal moves through it. The spatial coordinate is not time, and the model does not by itself describe memory drift, spike timing, or learning.]{.key-statement} ## Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fields {#sec:PLACE-GP} To predict a field's width, we need to relate activity at nearby positions. A histogram of firing rates alone loses that information: rearranging its values could turn one broad field into many tiny fields without changing the histogram. The model assigns an input $h(x)$ to each position $x$, with nearby values linked so that a cell can have a continuous active region. [A **Gaussian process** specifies a distribution of such maps.]{.definition-explanation} Its mean sets the average input, and its spatial covariance describes how inputs at two positions vary together across possible maps. The chosen covariance must also make the maps smooth enough for the derivatives used below. After a map is drawn, moving the animal changes which position is evaluated, not the map itself. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Mathematical definitions: Gaussian processes and spatial covariance"} [A [**Gaussian process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a probability distribution over functions such that the values at any finite set of positions form a jointly Gaussian random vector.]{.definition-explanation} For positions $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the vector $(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_n))$ therefore has a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Its mean vector and covariance matrix are obtained by evaluating two functions, $$ m(x)=\mathbb E[h(x)],\qquad C(x,y)=\mathbb E[(h(x)-m(x))(h(y)-m(y))]. $$ The expectation runs over possible maps, or over cells assumed to share these statistics. These two functions determine every finite joint distribution. A Gaussian process can thus produce many different curves while keeping a precise rule for their spatial dependence. [A [**jointly Gaussian vector**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is one for which every linear combination of its entries is Gaussian.]{.definition-explanation} For this family, zero covariance between two subvectors implies their independence. That extra property, which does not hold for general distributions, will simplify the crossing calculation. The values after thresholding will generally not have a Gaussian distribution.[^p3-model] ::: Three assumptions have different jobs: - [[**Stationarity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that moving the observation window does not change the map's probability law. Here it gives a constant mean and a covariance $C(x,y)=C(y-x)$ that depends on separation.]{.definition-explanation} It does not say that a particular map is flat. - [[**Isotropy**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that rotating the separation does not change the covariance: in several dimensions, $C(\Delta x)$ depends only on $\|\Delta x\|$.]{.definition-explanation} It rules out a preferred direction in the model's statistics. Stationarity alone does not imply isotropy. - [[**Smoothness**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} controls whether the map has well defined spatial derivatives.]{.definition-explanation} Crossing calculations require differentiable sample functions and nondegenerate joint distributions: the relevant vector of heights and derivatives must have an invertible covariance matrix, rather than obey an exact linear constraint. Peak calculations require second derivatives and enough regularity to control their local approximation. A Gaussian distribution of values does not guarantee this smoothness. For example, a covariance proportional to $e^{-|x-y|/b}$ has a sharp corner at zero separation and does not supply the differentiable paths assumed below. Set the mean to zero and write $\sigma_h^2=C(0)$ for input variance. A constant input mean can be absorbed into the threshold. It is useful to normalize the input, $$ z(x)=\frac{h(x)}{\sigma_h},\qquad F(x)=a\,[z(x)-q]_+, \quad [u]_+=\max(u,0). $$ Here $z$ has variance one, $q$ is a dimensionless threshold, and $a>0$ converts normalized input to firing rate, in Hz. The paper writes $\theta$ for $q$, $r$ for covariance, and $D$ for spatial dimension; this guide uses $q,C,d$ to avoid conflicts with earlier chapters. The original input threshold is $q\sigma_h$. In the paper's Equation 3 the firing rate is proportional to $[h-q\sigma_h]_+$, which is equivalent to this form after choosing the gain.[^p3-model] The input threshold summarizes how much combined input is needed before the model cell fires. It can reflect the cell's own response properties and inhibitory input. Raising $q$ at a fixed input map leaves fewer positions active. If the absolute threshold above the input mean is positive and held fixed, increasing the input standard deviation $\sigma_h$ lowers $q$, making activity more widespread. Changing $a$ instead changes rates within active regions while preserving their zero-rate boundaries. A fixed positive detection cutoff in Hz would change this last conclusion. [A fitted threshold describes the balance of input and response; it does not identify which biological quantity changed.]{.key-statement}
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 1
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-1}}
[The [**excursion set**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} above $q$ is]{.definition-explanation} $$ A_q=\{x:z(x)>q\}. $$ Each connected piece of $A_q$ is a model place field. In one dimension its size is length. In two and three dimensions it is area and volume. [Two nearby peaks belong to one field if an above-threshold path joins them. Counting peaks and counting fields therefore answer different questions.]{.key-statement} For a one dimensional stationary process, differentiation of covariance gives $$ \operatorname{Var}(h')= \left.\partial_x\partial_y C(y-x)\right|_{y=x}=-C''(0). $$ The minus sign comes from differentiating $y-x$ once with respect to each variable. The paper defines the spatial scale $$ \sigma=\sqrt{-\frac{C(0)}{C''(0)}}; \qquad \operatorname{Var}(z')=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}. $$ Thus $\sigma$ compares typical height with typical slope and has units of distance. In an isotropic field, the same definition applies along any unit direction. For the smooth Gaussian covariance $C(\Delta x)=\sigma_h^2\exp[-\|\Delta x\|^2/(2\sigma^2)]$, it is exactly the parameter in that exponent. The paper uses a Gaussian covariance for its simulations. Other smooth covariances can share this local scale while having different longer distance structure.[^p3-scale] A simulated Gaussian input map with covariance $C(\Delta x)=\exp[-(\Delta x/\sigma)^2/2]$ gives the firing map below when $q=0.8$ and $a=6$ Hz. Position is shown in units of $\sigma$.
{{block:fig:PLACE-GP-TO-FIRING}}
Thresholding changes the distribution of values and can separate one smooth input curve into several fields. Both panels describe the same fixed map over space, so neither curve is a trajectory over time. See [Gaussian input and firing rate, STAR Methods Eqs. 2–3, p. e1](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=13). ## Upcrossings count fields, with an endpoint correction {#sec:PLACE-KAC-RICE} A field starts at an upcrossing, so its expected count can be found by counting upward passages through the threshold. A small interval around each crossing has a width determined by its slope; this lets us count crossings without locating every root. Consider a differentiable fixed curve and a simple upward crossing $x_0$ of $q$, with slope $v=z'(x_0)>0$. Close to the crossing, $$ z(x)-q\simeq v(x-x_0). $$ The curve lies in the vertical band $|z-q|<\varepsilon$ for a spatial distance approximately $2\varepsilon/v$. Integrating $z'(x)/(2\varepsilon)$ over that interval contributes one. Restricting to positive slopes counts only upward crossings. [Under the usual regularity conditions, averaging this counting identity gives the [**Kac–Rice formula**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} for the mean upcrossing density,]{.definition-explanation} $$ \nu_+(q)=\int_0^\infty v\,p_{z,z'}(q,v)\,dv. $$ The density $p_{z,z'}(q,v)$ describes how often height is near $q$ and slope near $v$. Multiplication by $v$ compensates for the shorter spatial window of a steep crossing. Multiplying the probability of being above threshold by a typical slope would miss this weighting.[^p3-crossings] A fixed smooth curve shows how to count a field already active at the left edge and why the crossing integral weights each slope.
{{block:fig:PLACE-CROSSINGS}}
The count includes every connected active interval intersecting the track. Discarding clipped boundary fields would change this convention. We can evaluate the integral because height and slope are independent here. Stationarity gives $$ \mathbb E[zz']=\frac12\frac{d}{dx}\mathbb E[z(x)^2]=0. $$ Height and slope are jointly Gaussian; zero covariance therefore makes them independent. Their distributions are $z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and $z'\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^{-2})$. Consequently, $$ \begin{aligned} \nu_+(q) &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_0^\infty v\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\sigma^2v^2/2}\,dv\\ &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} =\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\sigma}. \end{aligned} $$ In the integral, use $u=\sigma^2v^2/2$, so $v\,dv=du/\sigma^2$. [This result is exact for the stated smooth stationary Gaussian model. A high threshold is not needed.]{.key-statement} Its units are inverse distance: increasing $\sigma$ stretches the map and reduces crossings per metre. On a finite track $[0,L]$, each upcrossing starts a field, but a field may already be active at the left endpoint. If $N_L$ counts all components intersecting the track, then, under regularity conditions that exclude tangencies and give nonzero slopes at crossings, $$ N_L=N_+(q;[0,L])+\mathbf1\{z(0)>q\}, \qquad \mathbb E[N_L]=L\nu_+(q)+Q(q), $$ where $Q(q)=1-\Phi(q)$ and $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The last term is the endpoint correction. Removing incomplete boundary fields changes the counting convention, so the same correction cannot then be used unchanged. This identity also gives the paper's exact one dimensional mean Euler characteristic, Equation 8.[^p3-ec-source] ## Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scale {#sec:PLACE-INFERENCE} [A low field count can result from a high threshold or a slowly varying map. Field lengths help separate those possibilities.]{.key-statement} At a uniformly chosen position, the probability of activity is $Q(q)$. Hence a track of length $L$ has expected occupied length $LQ(q)$. On a long stationary track, the average occupied length per field is the occupied length per unit distance divided by the number of fields per unit distance. The corresponding gap calculation uses the inactive fraction $\Phi(q)$: $$ \begin{aligned} \mu_s&=\frac{Q(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma Q(q)e^{q^2/2},\\ \mu_g&=\frac{\Phi(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma\Phi(q)e^{q^2/2}. \end{aligned} $$ These are stationary per-field and per-gap means, ignoring clipping at track boundaries. They are not an assertion that the expectation of a finite sample's ratio equals the ratio of its expectations. Subject to suitable averaging over a long track or many maps, they give the inference rule in Methods S3, Equations S14–S15.[^p3-means] Adding and dividing removes one unknown at a time: $$ \mu_s+\mu_g=2\pi\sigma e^{q^2/2},\qquad \frac{\mu_s}{\mu_s+\mu_g}=Q(q). $$ Thus $$ q=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\mu_g}{\mu_s+\mu_g}\right), \qquad \sigma=\frac{\mu_s+\mu_g}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2}. $$ For example, $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m, the fitted parameters reported for the 200 m bat tunnel, give $Q(q)=0.1357$, $\nu_+=0.03621$ per metre, $\mu_s=3.746$ m, and $\mu_g=23.868$ m in the continuous model. Putting these two means into the inversion recovers $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m. The expected number of intersecting fields on a 200 m track is $7.2425+0.1357=7.3782$, including the left endpoint term. These are calculations from the fitted model, not fresh estimates from raw recordings. [The means do not imply a full gap or count distribution. At high thresholds, distant rare excursions can approach independent events if correlations decay sufficiently with distance. In that regime, field locations approach a Poisson process, counts in a long interval are approximately Poisson, and gaps are approximately exponential. Smoothness and stationarity alone do not ensure this independence.]{.key-statement} A periodic Gaussian process, for example, retains long distance dependence. Upward and downward crossings that enclose the same small field remain strongly related even when fields far apart are almost independent. Experimental selection also matters. If cells with no fields are excluded, a Poisson model with unconditioned mean $\lambda$ gives $$ \Pr(N=n\mid N\ge1)= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n}{n!(1-e^{-\lambda})},\quad n\ge1, \qquad \mathbb E[N\mid N\ge1]=\frac{\lambda}{1-e^{-\lambda}}. $$ The mean follows because the omitted $n=0$ term contributes zero to $\sum n\Pr(N=n)=\lambda$, while conditioning divides all remaining probabilities by $1-e^{-\lambda}$. For $\lambda=1$, $36.8\%$ of cells are excluded and the observed mean is $1.582$, not one. Using $1.582$ as the unconditioned mean would infer too many fields. The paper applies this correction to its two dimensional count fit, Equation 5.[^p3-selection] [^p3-question]: Mainali, N., Azeredo da Silveira, R., & Burak, Y. (2025). *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*. Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), Introduction and Results, pp. 1110–1111; Figure 1. [^p3-model]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), STAR Methods, Equations 2–3, p. e1; Supplemental Methods S1, p. 8. Here it gives a constant mean and a covariance $C(x,y)=C(y-x)$ that depends on separation.]{.definition-explanation} It does not say that a particular map is flat. - [[**Isotropy**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that rotating the separation does not change the covariance: in several dimensions, $C(\Delta x)$ depends only on $\|\Delta x\|$.]{.definition-explanation} It rules out a preferred direction in the model's statistics. For example, a covariance proportional to $e^{-|x-y|/b}$ has a sharp corner at zero separation and does not supply the differentiable paths assumed below. Set the mean to zero and write $\sigma_h^2=C(0)$ for input variance. A constant input mean can be absorbed into the threshold. It is useful to normalize the input, $$ z(x)=\frac{h(x)}{\sigma_h},\qquad F(x)=a\,[z(x)-q]_+, \quad [u]_+=\max(u,0). $$ Here $z$ has variance one, $q$ is a dimensionless threshold, and $a>0$ converts normalized input to firing rate, in Hz. In the paper's Equation 3 the firing rate is proportional to $[h-q\sigma_h]_+$, which is equivalent to this form after choosing the gain.[^p3-model] The input threshold summarizes how much combined input is needed before the model cell fires. It can reflect the cell's own response properties and inhibitory input. Raising $q$ at a fixed input map leaves fewer positions active. If the absolute threshold above the input mean is positive and held fixed, increasing the input standard deviation $\sigma_h$ lowers $q$, making activity more widespread. Changing $a$ instead changes rates within active regions while preserving their zero-rate boundaries. A fixed positive detection cutoff in Hz would change this last conclusion. [A fitted threshold describes the balance of input and response; it does not identify which biological quantity changed.]{.key-statement}

{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-1}}
[The [**excursion set**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} above $q$ is]{.definition-explanation} $$ A_q=\{x:z(x)>q\}. $$ Each connected piece of $A_q$ is a model place field. In one dimension its size is length. In two and three dimensions it is area and volume. [Two nearby peaks belong to one field if an above-threshold path joins them. Counting peaks and counting fields therefore answer different questions.]{.key-statement} For a one dimensional stationary process, differentiation of covariance gives $$ \operatorname{Var}(h')= \left.\partial_x\partial_y C(y-x)\right|_{y=x}=-C''(0). $$ The minus sign comes from differentiating $y-x$ once with respect to each variable. The paper defines the spatial scale $$ \sigma=\sqrt{-\frac{C(0)}{C''(0)}}; \qquad \operatorname{Var}(z')=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}. $$ Thus $\sigma$ compares typical height with typical slope and has units of distance. In an isotropic field, the same definition applies along any unit direction. For the smooth Gaussian covariance $C(\Delta x)=\sigma_h^2\exp[-\|\Delta x\|^2/(2\sigma^2)]$, it is exactly the parameter in that exponent. The paper uses a Gaussian covariance for its simulations. Other smooth covariances can share this local scale while having different longer distance structure.[^p3-scale] A simulated Gaussian input map with covariance $C(\Delta x)=\exp[-(\Delta x/\sigma)^2/2]$ gives the firing map below when $q=0.8$ and $a=6$ Hz. Position is shown in units of $\sigma$.
{{block:fig:PLACE-GP-TO-FIRING}}
Thresholding changes the distribution of values and can separate one smooth input curve into several fields. Both panels describe the same fixed map over space, so neither curve is a trajectory over time. See [Gaussian input and firing rate, STAR Methods Eqs. 2–3, p. e1](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=13).

review_metadata.title: Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale
review_metadata.purpose: Hippocampal place cells fire more at particular locations as an animal moves. This chapter introduces the rodent and bat recordings, then shows how a smooth random input that exceeds a firing threshold can produce several separate active regions for one cell.

section_list.title: Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fields
section_list.summary: To predict a field's width, we need to relate activity at nearby positions. A histogram of firing rates alone loses that information: rearranging its values could turn one broad field into many tiny fields without changing the histogram.

section_list.title: Upcrossings count fields, with an endpoint correction
section_list.summary: A field starts at an upcrossing, so its expected count can be found by counting upward passages through the threshold. A small interval around each crossing has a width determined by its slope; this lets us count crossings without locating every root.

section_list.title: Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scale
section_list.summary: A low field count can result from a high threshold or a slowly varying map. Field lengths help separate those possibilities.

How could one model produce this variety and still make useful predictions?]{.key-statement} Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak propose that a cell's spatial input is a smooth random function. This function can be interpreted as the average combined input arriving through the cell's synapses at each animal position. The model cell has positive firing rate where this input exceeds a threshold. The recordings estimate firing rates rather than measuring this input directly.[^p3-model] [The model predicts distributions of field lengths, areas, and volumes, rather than the location of a particular cell's next field. Combining that count with the lengths of active fields and inactive gaps then separates the effect of the threshold from the distance over which the map changes. These calculations establish the parameters needed for the later predictions of sizes and shapes. [Spatial randomness here describes different possible rate maps. Once a map is drawn, it is fixed while the animal moves through it. The spatial coordinate is not time, and the model does not by itself describe memory drift, spike timing, or learning.]{.key-statement} ## Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fields {#sec:PLACE-GP} To predict a field's width, we need to relate activity at nearby positions. These two functions determine every finite joint distribution. A Gaussian process can thus produce many different curves while keeping a precise rule for their spatial dependence. [A [**jointly Gaussian vector**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is one for which every linear combination of its entries is Gaussian.]{.definition-explanation} For this family, zero covariance between two subvectors implies their independence. That extra property, which does not hold for general distributions, will simplify the crossing calculation. The paper writes $\theta$ for $q$, $r$ for covariance, and $D$ for spatial dimension; this guide uses $q,C,d$ to avoid conflicts with earlier chapters. The original input threshold is $q\sigma_h$. [The [**excursion set**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} above $q$ is]{.definition-explanation} $$ A_q=\{x:z(x)>q\}. $$ Each connected piece of $A_q$ is a model place field. In one dimension its size is length. In two and three dimensions it is area and volume. [Two nearby peaks belong to one field if an above-threshold path joins them. Counting peaks and counting fields therefore answer different questions.]{.key-statement} For a one dimensional stationary process, differentiation of covariance gives $$ \operatorname{Var}(h')= \left.\partial_x\partial_y C(y-x)\right|_{y=x}=-C''(0). $$ The minus sign comes from differentiating $y-x$ once with respect to each variable. The paper defines the spatial scale $$ \sigma=\sqrt{-\frac{C(0)}{C''(0)}}; \qquad \operatorname{Var}(z')=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}. $$ Thus $\sigma$ compares typical height with typical slope and has units of distance. In an isotropic field, the same definition applies along any unit direction. For the smooth Gaussian covariance $C(\Delta x)=\sigma_h^2\exp[-\|\Delta x\|^2/(2\sigma^2)]$, it is exactly the parameter in that exponent. The paper uses a Gaussian covariance for its simulations. Other smooth covariances can share this local scale while having different longer distance structure.[^p3-scale] A simulated Gaussian input map with covariance $C(\Delta x)=\exp[-(\Delta x/\sigma)^2/2]$ gives the firing map below when $q=0.8$ and $a=6$ Hz. Position is shown in units of $\sigma$.
{{block:fig:PLACE-GP-TO-FIRING}}
Thresholding changes the distribution of values and can separate one smooth input curve into several fields. Both panels describe the same fixed map over space, so neither curve is a trajectory over time. See [Gaussian input and firing rate, STAR Methods Eqs. 2–3, p. e1](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=13). ## Upcrossings count fields, with an endpoint correction {#sec:PLACE-KAC-RICE} A field starts at an upcrossing, so its expected count can be found by counting upward passages through the threshold. A small interval around each crossing has a width determined by its slope; this lets us count crossings without locating every root. Consider a differentiable fixed curve and a simple upward crossing $x_0$ of $q$, with slope $v=z'(x_0)>0$. Close to the crossing, $$ z(x)-q\simeq v(x-x_0). $$ The curve lies in the vertical band $|z-q|<\varepsilon$ for a spatial distance approximately $2\varepsilon/v$. Integrating $z'(x)/(2\varepsilon)$ over that interval contributes one. Restricting to positive slopes counts only upward crossings. [Under the usual regularity conditions, averaging this counting identity gives the [**Kac–Rice formula**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} for the mean upcrossing density,]{.definition-explanation} $$ \nu_+(q)=\int_0^\infty v\,p_{z,z'}(q,v)\,dv. $$ The density $p_{z,z'}(q,v)$ describes how often height is near $q$ and slope near $v$. Multiplication by $v$ compensates for the shorter spatial window of a steep crossing. Multiplying the probability of being above threshold by a typical slope would miss this weighting.[^p3-crossings] A fixed smooth curve shows how to count a field already active at the left edge and why the crossing integral weights each slope.
{{block:fig:PLACE-CROSSINGS}}
The count includes every connected active interval intersecting the track. Discarding clipped boundary fields would change this convention. We can evaluate the integral because height and slope are independent here. Stationarity gives $$ \mathbb E[zz']=\frac12\frac{d}{dx}\mathbb E[z(x)^2]=0. $$ Height and slope are jointly Gaussian; zero covariance therefore makes them independent. Their distributions are $z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and $z'\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^{-2})$. Consequently, $$ \begin{aligned} \nu_+(q) &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_0^\infty v\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\sigma^2v^2/2}\,dv\\ &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} =\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\sigma}. \end{aligned} $$ In the integral, use $u=\sigma^2v^2/2$, so $v\,dv=du/\sigma^2$. [This result is exact for the stated smooth stationary Gaussian model. A high threshold is not needed.]{.key-statement} Its units are inverse distance: increasing $\sigma$ stretches the map and reduces crossings per metre. On a finite track $[0,L]$, each upcrossing starts a field, but a field may already be active at the left endpoint. If $N_L$ counts all components intersecting the track, then, under regularity conditions that exclude tangencies and give nonzero slopes at crossings, $$ N_L=N_+(q;[0,L])+\mathbf1\{z(0)>q\}, \qquad \mathbb E[N_L]=L\nu_+(q)+Q(q), $$ where $Q(q)=1-\Phi(q)$ and $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The last term is the endpoint correction. Removing incomplete boundary fields changes the counting convention, so the same correction cannot then be used unchanged. This identity also gives the paper's exact one dimensional mean Euler characteristic, Equation 8.[^p3-ec-source] ## Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scale {#sec:PLACE-INFERENCE} [A low field count can result from a high threshold or a slowly varying map. Field lengths help separate those possibilities.]{.key-statement} At a uniformly chosen position, the probability of activity is $Q(q)$. Hence a track of length $L$ has expected occupied length $LQ(q)$. On a long stationary track, the average occupied length per field is the occupied length per unit distance divided by the number of fields per unit distance. The corresponding gap calculation uses the inactive fraction $\Phi(q)$: $$ \begin{aligned} \mu_s&=\frac{Q(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma Q(q)e^{q^2/2},\\ \mu_g&=\frac{\Phi(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma\Phi(q)e^{q^2/2}. \end{aligned} $$ These are stationary per-field and per-gap means, ignoring clipping at track boundaries. They are not an assertion that the expectation of a finite sample's ratio equals the ratio of its expectations. Subject to suitable averaging over a long track or many maps, they give the inference rule in Methods S3, Equations S14–S15.[^p3-means] Adding and dividing removes one unknown at a time: $$ \mu_s+\mu_g=2\pi\sigma e^{q^2/2},\qquad \frac{\mu_s}{\mu_s+\mu_g}=Q(q). $$ Thus $$ q=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\mu_g}{\mu_s+\mu_g}\right), \qquad \sigma=\frac{\mu_s+\mu_g}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2}. $$ For example, $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m, the fitted parameters reported for the 200 m bat tunnel, give $Q(q)=0.1357$, $\nu_+=0.03621$ per metre, $\mu_s=3.746$ m, and $\mu_g=23.868$ m in the continuous model. Putting these two means into the inversion recovers $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m. The expected number of intersecting fields on a 200 m track is $7.2425+0.1357=7.3782$, including the left endpoint term. These are calculations from the fitted model, not fresh estimates from raw recordings. [The means do not imply a full gap or count distribution. At high thresholds, distant rare excursions can approach independent events if correlations decay sufficiently with distance. In that regime, field locations approach a Poisson process, counts in a long interval are approximately Poisson, and gaps are approximately exponential. Smoothness and stationarity alone do not ensure this independence.]{.key-statement} A periodic Gaussian process, for example, retains long distance dependence. Upward and downward crossings that enclose the same small field remain strongly related even when fields far apart are almost independent. Experimental selection also matters. If cells with no fields are excluded, a Poisson model with unconditioned mean $\lambda$ gives $$ \Pr(N=n\mid N\ge1)= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n}{n!(1-e^{-\lambda})},\quad n\ge1, \qquad \mathbb E[N\mid N\ge1]=\frac{\lambda}{1-e^{-\lambda}}. $$ The mean follows because the omitted $n=0$ term contributes zero to $\sum n\Pr(N=n)=\lambda$, while conditioning divides all remaining probabilities by $1-e^{-\lambda}$. For $\lambda=1$, $36.8\%$ of cells are excluded and the observed mean is $1.582$, not one. Using $1.582$ as the unconditioned mean would infer too many fields. ## Upcrossings count fields, with an endpoint correction {#sec:PLACE-KAC-RICE} A field starts at an upcrossing, so its expected count can be found by counting upward passages through the threshold. A small interval around each crossing has a width determined by its slope; this lets us count crossings without locating every root. Consider a differentiable fixed curve and a simple upward crossing $x_0$ of $q$, with slope $v=z'(x_0)>0$. Close to the crossing, $$ z(x)-q\simeq v(x-x_0). $$ The curve lies in the vertical band $|z-q|<\varepsilon$ for a spatial distance approximately $2\varepsilon/v$. Integrating $z'(x)/(2\varepsilon)$ over that interval contributes one. Restricting to positive slopes counts only upward crossings. [Under the usual regularity conditions, averaging this counting identity gives the [**Kac–Rice formula**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} for the mean upcrossing density,]{.definition-explanation} $$ \nu_+(q)=\int_0^\infty v\,p_{z,z'}(q,v)\,dv. $$ The density $p_{z,z'}(q,v)$ describes how often height is near $q$ and slope near $v$. Multiplication by $v$ compensates for the shorter spatial window of a steep crossing. Multiplying the probability of being above threshold by a typical slope would miss this weighting.[^p3-crossings] A fixed smooth curve shows how to count a field already active at the left edge and why the crossing integral weights each slope.
{{block:fig:PLACE-CROSSINGS}}
The count includes every connected active interval intersecting the track. Discarding clipped boundary fields would change this convention. We can evaluate the integral because height and slope are independent here. Stationarity gives $$ \mathbb E[zz']=\frac12\frac{d}{dx}\mathbb E[z(x)^2]=0. $$ Height and slope are jointly Gaussian; zero covariance therefore makes them independent. Their distributions are $z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and $z'\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^{-2})$. Consequently, $$ \begin{aligned} \nu_+(q) &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_0^\infty v\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\sigma^2v^2/2}\,dv\\ &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} =\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\sigma}. \end{aligned} $$ In the integral, use $u=\sigma^2v^2/2$, so $v\,dv=du/\sigma^2$. [This result is exact for the stated smooth stationary Gaussian model. A high threshold is not needed.]{.key-statement} Its units are inverse distance: increasing $\sigma$ stretches the map and reduces crossings per metre. On a finite track $[0,L]$, each upcrossing starts a field, but a field may already be active at the left endpoint. If $N_L$ counts all components intersecting the track, then, under regularity conditions that exclude tangencies and give nonzero slopes at crossings, $$ N_L=N_+(q;[0,L])+\mathbf1\{z(0)>q\}, \qquad \mathbb E[N_L]=L\nu_+(q)+Q(q), $$ where $Q(q)=1-\Phi(q)$ and $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The last term is the endpoint correction. Removing incomplete boundary fields changes the counting convention, so the same correction cannot then be used unchanged. This identity also gives the paper's exact one dimensional mean Euler characteristic, Equation 8.[^p3-ec-source]

review_metadata.title: Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale
review_metadata.purpose: Hippocampal place cells fire more at particular locations as an animal moves. This chapter introduces the rodent and bat recordings, then shows how a smooth random input that exceeds a firing threshold can produce several separate active regions for one cell.

section_list.summary: A low field count can result from a high threshold or a slowly varying map. Field lengths help separate those possibilities.
