# Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale {#ch:PLACE-FIELDS} The study compares recordings of hippocampal place cells from bats flying through tunnels, rats moving over an arena floor, and bats flying through a room. For tunnel flights, the analysis uses distance along an approximately one-dimensional route, although the tunnel itself has width and height. The floor map uses two position coordinates, and the room map uses three. A cell recorded on a short track may have one smooth firing hill. [On a long track, the same kind of cell may have several separated fields, each with a different width and height. In a room, its active regions can bend, split, and surround inactive holes. How could one model produce this variety and still make useful predictions?]{.key-statement} Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak propose that a cell's spatial input is a smooth random function. This function can be interpreted as the average combined input arriving through the cell's synapses at each animal position. The model cell has positive firing rate where this input exceeds a threshold. The recordings estimate firing rates rather than measuring this input directly.[^p3-model] [The model predicts distributions of field lengths, areas, and volumes, rather than the location of a particular cell's next field. Its strongest tests ask whether fitting field sizes and counts also explains field shapes and holes.]{.key-statement}[^p3-question] We begin on a track, where a field starts at [an [**upcrossing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a point where the input crosses upward through the threshold.]{.definition-explanation} Counting these crossings gives the average number of fields. Combining that count with the lengths of active fields and inactive gaps then separates the effect of the threshold from the distance over which the map changes. These calculations establish the parameters needed for the later predictions of sizes and shapes. [Spatial randomness here describes different possible rate maps. Once a map is drawn, it is fixed while the animal moves through it. The spatial coordinate is not time, and the model does not by itself describe memory drift, spike timing, or learning.]{.key-statement} ## Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fields {#sec:PLACE-GP} To predict a field's width, we need to relate activity at nearby positions. A histogram of firing rates alone loses that information: rearranging its values could turn one broad field into many tiny fields without changing the histogram. The model assigns an input $h(x)$ to each position $x$, with nearby values linked so that a cell can have a continuous active region. [A **Gaussian process** specifies a distribution of such maps.]{.definition-explanation} Its mean sets the average input, and its spatial covariance describes how inputs at two positions vary together across possible maps. The chosen covariance must also make the maps smooth enough for the derivatives used below. After a map is drawn, moving the animal changes which position is evaluated, not the map itself. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Mathematical definitions: Gaussian processes and spatial covariance"} [A [**Gaussian process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a probability distribution over functions such that the values at any finite set of positions form a jointly Gaussian random vector.]{.definition-explanation} For positions $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the vector $(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_n))$ therefore has a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Its mean vector and covariance matrix are obtained by evaluating two functions, $$ m(x)=\mathbb E[h(x)],\qquad C(x,y)=\mathbb E[(h(x)-m(x))(h(y)-m(y))]. $$ The expectation runs over possible maps, or over cells assumed to share these statistics. These two functions determine every finite joint distribution. A Gaussian process can thus produce many different curves while keeping a precise rule for their spatial dependence. [A [**jointly Gaussian vector**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is one for which every linear combination of its entries is Gaussian.]{.definition-explanation} For this family, zero covariance between two subvectors implies their independence. That extra property, which does not hold for general distributions, will simplify the crossing calculation. The values after thresholding will generally not have a Gaussian distribution.[^p3-model] ::: Three assumptions have different jobs: - [[**Stationarity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that moving the observation window does not change the map's probability law. Here it gives a constant mean and a covariance $C(x,y)=C(y-x)$ that depends on separation.]{.definition-explanation} It does not say that a particular map is flat. - [[**Isotropy**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that rotating the separation does not change the covariance: in several dimensions, $C(\Delta x)$ depends only on $\|\Delta x\|$.]{.definition-explanation} It rules out a preferred direction in the model's statistics. Stationarity alone does not imply isotropy. - [[**Smoothness**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} controls whether the map has well defined spatial derivatives.]{.definition-explanation} Crossing calculations require differentiable sample functions and nondegenerate joint distributions: the relevant vector of heights and derivatives must have an invertible covariance matrix, rather than obey an exact linear constraint. Peak calculations require second derivatives and enough regularity to control their local approximation. A Gaussian distribution of values does not guarantee this smoothness. For example, a covariance proportional to $e^{-|x-y|/b}$ has a sharp corner at zero separation and does not supply the differentiable paths assumed below. Set the mean to zero and write $\sigma_h^2=C(0)$ for input variance. A constant input mean can be absorbed into the threshold. It is useful to normalize the input, $$ z(x)=\frac{h(x)}{\sigma_h},\qquad F(x)=a\,[z(x)-q]_+, \quad [u]_+=\max(u,0). $$ Here $z$ has variance one, $q$ is a dimensionless threshold, and $a>0$ converts normalized input to firing rate, in Hz. The paper writes $\theta$ for $q$, $r$ for covariance, and $D$ for spatial dimension; this guide uses $q,C,d$ to avoid conflicts with earlier chapters. The original input threshold is $q\sigma_h$. In the paper's Equation 3 the firing rate is proportional to $[h-q\sigma_h]_+$, which is equivalent to this form after choosing the gain.[^p3-model] The input threshold summarizes how much combined input is needed before the model cell fires. It can reflect the cell's own response properties and inhibitory input. Raising $q$ at a fixed input map leaves fewer positions active. If the absolute threshold above the input mean is positive and held fixed, increasing the input standard deviation $\sigma_h$ lowers $q$, making activity more widespread. Changing $a$ instead changes rates within active regions while preserving their zero-rate boundaries. A fixed positive detection cutoff in Hz would change this last conclusion. [A fitted threshold describes the balance of input and response; it does not identify which biological quantity changed.]{.key-statement}
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 1
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-1}}
[The [**excursion set**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} above $q$ is]{.definition-explanation} $$ A_q=\{x:z(x)>q\}. $$ Each connected piece of $A_q$ is a model place field. In one dimension its size is length. In two and three dimensions it is area and volume. [Two nearby peaks belong to one field if an above-threshold path joins them. Counting peaks and counting fields therefore answer different questions.]{.key-statement} For a one dimensional stationary process, differentiation of covariance gives $$ \operatorname{Var}(h')= \left.\partial_x\partial_y C(y-x)\right|_{y=x}=-C''(0). $$ The minus sign comes from differentiating $y-x$ once with respect to each variable. The paper defines the spatial scale $$ \sigma=\sqrt{-\frac{C(0)}{C''(0)}}; \qquad \operatorname{Var}(z')=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}. $$ Thus $\sigma$ compares typical height with typical slope and has units of distance. In an isotropic field, the same definition applies along any unit direction. For the smooth Gaussian covariance $C(\Delta x)=\sigma_h^2\exp[-\|\Delta x\|^2/(2\sigma^2)]$, it is exactly the parameter in that exponent. The paper uses a Gaussian covariance for its simulations. Other smooth covariances can share this local scale while having different longer distance structure.[^p3-scale] A simulated Gaussian input map with covariance $C(\Delta x)=\exp[-(\Delta x/\sigma)^2/2]$ gives the firing map below when $q=0.8$ and $a=6$ Hz. Position is shown in units of $\sigma$.
{{block:fig:PLACE-GP-TO-FIRING}}
Thresholding changes the distribution of values and can separate one smooth input curve into several fields. Both panels describe the same fixed map over space, so neither curve is a trajectory over time. See [Gaussian input and firing rate, STAR Methods Eqs. 2–3, p. e1](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=13). ## Upcrossings count fields, with an endpoint correction {#sec:PLACE-KAC-RICE} A field starts at an upcrossing, so its expected count can be found by counting upward passages through the threshold. A small interval around each crossing has a width determined by its slope; this lets us count crossings without locating every root. Consider a differentiable fixed curve and a simple upward crossing $x_0$ of $q$, with slope $v=z'(x_0)>0$. Close to the crossing, $$ z(x)-q\simeq v(x-x_0). $$ The curve lies in the vertical band $|z-q|<\varepsilon$ for a spatial distance approximately $2\varepsilon/v$. Integrating $z'(x)/(2\varepsilon)$ over that interval contributes one. Restricting to positive slopes counts only upward crossings. [Under the usual regularity conditions, averaging this counting identity gives the [**Kac–Rice formula**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} for the mean upcrossing density,]{.definition-explanation} $$ \nu_+(q)=\int_0^\infty v\,p_{z,z'}(q,v)\,dv. $$ The density $p_{z,z'}(q,v)$ describes how often height is near $q$ and slope near $v$. Multiplication by $v$ compensates for the shorter spatial window of a steep crossing. Multiplying the probability of being above threshold by a typical slope would miss this weighting.[^p3-crossings] A fixed smooth curve shows how to count a field already active at the left edge and why the crossing integral weights each slope.
{{block:fig:PLACE-CROSSINGS}}
The count includes every connected active interval intersecting the track. Discarding clipped boundary fields would change this convention. We can evaluate the integral because height and slope are independent here. Stationarity gives $$ \mathbb E[zz']=\frac12\frac{d}{dx}\mathbb E[z(x)^2]=0. $$ Height and slope are jointly Gaussian; zero covariance therefore makes them independent. Their distributions are $z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and $z'\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^{-2})$. Consequently, $$ \begin{aligned} \nu_+(q) &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_0^\infty v\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\sigma^2v^2/2}\,dv\\ &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} =\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\sigma}. \end{aligned} $$ In the integral, use $u=\sigma^2v^2/2$, so $v\,dv=du/\sigma^2$. [This result is exact for the stated smooth stationary Gaussian model. A high threshold is not needed.]{.key-statement} Its units are inverse distance: increasing $\sigma$ stretches the map and reduces crossings per metre. On a finite track $[0,L]$, each upcrossing starts a field, but a field may already be active at the left endpoint. If $N_L$ counts all components intersecting the track, then, under regularity conditions that exclude tangencies and give nonzero slopes at crossings, $$ N_L=N_+(q;[0,L])+\mathbf1\{z(0)>q\}, \qquad \mathbb E[N_L]=L\nu_+(q)+Q(q), $$ where $Q(q)=1-\Phi(q)$ and $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The last term is the endpoint correction. Removing incomplete boundary fields changes the counting convention, so the same correction cannot then be used unchanged. This identity also gives the paper's exact one dimensional mean Euler characteristic, Equation 8.[^p3-ec-source] ## Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scale {#sec:PLACE-INFERENCE} [A low field count can result from a high threshold or a slowly varying map. Field lengths help separate those possibilities.]{.key-statement} At a uniformly chosen position, the probability of activity is $Q(q)$. Hence a track of length $L$ has expected occupied length $LQ(q)$. On a long stationary track, the average occupied length per field is the occupied length per unit distance divided by the number of fields per unit distance. The corresponding gap calculation uses the inactive fraction $\Phi(q)$: $$ \begin{aligned} \mu_s&=\frac{Q(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma Q(q)e^{q^2/2},\\ \mu_g&=\frac{\Phi(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma\Phi(q)e^{q^2/2}. \end{aligned} $$ These are stationary per-field and per-gap means, ignoring clipping at track boundaries. They are not an assertion that the expectation of a finite sample's ratio equals the ratio of its expectations. Subject to suitable averaging over a long track or many maps, they give the inference rule in Methods S3, Equations S14–S15.[^p3-means] Adding and dividing removes one unknown at a time: $$ \mu_s+\mu_g=2\pi\sigma e^{q^2/2},\qquad \frac{\mu_s}{\mu_s+\mu_g}=Q(q). $$ Thus $$ q=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\mu_g}{\mu_s+\mu_g}\right), \qquad \sigma=\frac{\mu_s+\mu_g}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2}. $$ For example, $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m, the fitted parameters reported for the 200 m bat tunnel, give $Q(q)=0.1357$, $\nu_+=0.03621$ per metre, $\mu_s=3.746$ m, and $\mu_g=23.868$ m in the continuous model. Putting these two means into the inversion recovers $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m. The expected number of intersecting fields on a 200 m track is $7.2425+0.1357=7.3782$, including the left endpoint term. These are calculations from the fitted model, not fresh estimates from raw recordings. [The means do not imply a full gap or count distribution. At high thresholds, distant rare excursions can approach independent events if correlations decay sufficiently with distance. In that regime, field locations approach a Poisson process, counts in a long interval are approximately Poisson, and gaps are approximately exponential. Smoothness and stationarity alone do not ensure this independence.]{.key-statement} A periodic Gaussian process, for example, retains long distance dependence. Upward and downward crossings that enclose the same small field remain strongly related even when fields far apart are almost independent. Experimental selection also matters. If cells with no fields are excluded, a Poisson model with unconditioned mean $\lambda$ gives $$ \Pr(N=n\mid N\ge1)= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n}{n!(1-e^{-\lambda})},\quad n\ge1, \qquad \mathbb E[N\mid N\ge1]=\frac{\lambda}{1-e^{-\lambda}}. $$ The mean follows because the omitted $n=0$ term contributes zero to $\sum n\Pr(N=n)=\lambda$, while conditioning divides all remaining probabilities by $1-e^{-\lambda}$. For $\lambda=1$, $36.8\%$ of cells are excluded and the observed mean is $1.582$, not one. Using $1.582$ as the unconditioned mean would infer too many fields. The paper applies this correction to its two dimensional count fit, Equation 5.[^p3-selection] [^p3-question]: Mainali, N., Azeredo da Silveira, R., & Burak, Y. ## Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scale {#sec:PLACE-INFERENCE}

[A low field count can result from a high threshold or a slowly varying map. Field lengths help separate those possibilities.]{.key-statement}

At a uniformly chosen position, the probability of activity is $Q(q)$. Hence a track of length $L$ has expected occupied length $LQ(q)$. On a long stationary track, the average occupied length per field is the occupied length per unit distance divided by the number of fields per unit distance. The corresponding gap calculation uses the inactive fraction $\Phi(q)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_s&=\frac{Q(q)}{\nu_+(q)}
      =2\pi\sigma Q(q)e^{q^2/2},\\
\mu_g&=\frac{\Phi(q)}{\nu_+(q)}
      =2\pi\sigma\Phi(q)e^{q^2/2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

These are stationary per-field and per-gap means, ignoring clipping at track boundaries. They are not an assertion that the expectation of a finite sample's ratio equals the ratio of its expectations. Subject to suitable averaging over a long track or many maps, they give the inference rule in Methods S3, Equations S14–S15.[^p3-means]

Adding and dividing removes one unknown at a time:

$$
\mu_s+\mu_g=2\pi\sigma e^{q^2/2},\qquad
\frac{\mu_s}{\mu_s+\mu_g}=Q(q).
$$

Thus

$$
q=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\mu_g}{\mu_s+\mu_g}\right),
\qquad
\sigma=\frac{\mu_s+\mu_g}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2}.
$$

For example, $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m, the fitted parameters reported for the 200 m bat tunnel, give $Q(q)=0.1357$, $\nu_+=0.03621$ per metre, $\mu_s=3.746$ m, and $\mu_g=23.868$ m in the continuous model. Putting these two means into the inversion recovers $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m. The expected number of intersecting fields on a 200 m track is $7.2425+0.1357=7.3782$, including the left endpoint term. These are calculations from the fitted model, not fresh estimates from raw recordings.

[The means do not imply a full gap or count distribution. At high thresholds, distant rare excursions can approach independent events if correlations decay sufficiently with distance. In that regime, field locations approach a Poisson process, counts in a long interval are approximately Poisson, and gaps are approximately exponential. Smoothness and stationarity alone do not ensure this independence.]{.key-statement} A periodic Gaussian process, for example, retains long distance dependence. Upward and downward crossings that enclose the same small field remain strongly related even when fields far apart are almost independent.

Experimental selection also matters. If cells with no fields are excluded, a Poisson model with unconditioned mean $\lambda$ gives

$$
\Pr(N=n\mid N\ge1)=
\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n}{n!(1-e^{-\lambda})},\quad n\ge1,
\qquad
\mathbb E[N\mid N\ge1]=\frac{\lambda}{1-e^{-\lambda}}.
$$

The mean follows because the omitted $n=0$ term contributes zero to $\sum n\Pr(N=n)=\lambda$, while conditioning divides all remaining probabilities by $1-e^{-\lambda}$. For $\lambda=1$, $36.8\%$ of cells are excluded and the observed mean is $1.582$, not one. Using $1.582$ as the unconditioned mean would infer too many fields. The paper applies this correction to its two dimensional count fit, Equation 5.[^p3-selection]

review_metadata.title: Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale
review_metadata.purpose: Hippocampal place cells fire more at particular locations as an animal moves. This chapter introduces the rodent and bat recordings, then shows how a smooth random input that exceeds a firing threshold can produce several separate active regions for one cell.

# Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale {#ch:PLACE-FIELDS} The study compares recordings of hippocampal place cells from bats flying through tunnels, rats moving over an arena floor, and bats flying through a room. For tunnel flights, the analysis uses distance along an approximately one-dimensional route, although the tunnel itself has width and height. The floor map uses two position coordinates, and the room map uses three. A cell recorded on a short track may have one smooth firing hill. [On a long track, the same kind of cell may have several separated fields, each with a different width and height. In a room, its active regions can bend, split, and surround inactive holes. How could one model produce this variety and still make useful predictions?]{.key-statement} Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak propose that a cell's spatial input is a smooth random function. This function can be interpreted as the average combined input arriving through the cell's synapses at each animal position. The model cell has positive firing rate where this input exceeds a threshold. The recordings estimate firing rates rather than measuring this input directly.[^p3-model] [The model predicts distributions of field lengths, areas, and volumes, rather than the location of a particular cell's next field. Its strongest tests ask whether fitting field sizes and counts also explains field shapes and holes.]{.key-statement}[^p3-question] We begin on a track, where a field starts at [an [**upcrossing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a point where the input crosses upward through the threshold.]{.definition-explanation} Counting these crossings gives the average number of fields. Combining that count with the lengths of active fields and inactive gaps then separates the effect of the threshold from the distance over which the map changes. These calculations establish the parameters needed for the later predictions of sizes and shapes. [Spatial randomness here describes different possible rate maps. Once a map is drawn, it is fixed while the animal moves through it. The spatial coordinate is not time, and the model does not by itself describe memory drift, spike timing, or learning.]{.key-statement} ## Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fields {#sec:PLACE-GP} To predict a field's width, we need to relate activity at nearby positions. A histogram of firing rates alone loses that information: rearranging its values could turn one broad field into many tiny fields without changing the histogram. The model assigns an input $h(x)$ to each position $x$, with nearby values linked so that a cell can have a continuous active region. [A **Gaussian process** specifies a distribution of such maps.]{.definition-explanation} Its mean sets the average input, and its spatial covariance describes how inputs at two positions vary together across possible maps. The chosen covariance must also make the maps smooth enough for the derivatives used below. After a map is drawn, moving the animal changes which position is evaluated, not the map itself. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Mathematical definitions: Gaussian processes and spatial covariance"} [A [**Gaussian process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a probability distribution over functions such that the values at any finite set of positions form a jointly Gaussian random vector.]{.definition-explanation} For positions $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the vector $(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_n))$ therefore has a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Its mean vector and covariance matrix are obtained by evaluating two functions, $$ m(x)=\mathbb E[h(x)],\qquad C(x,y)=\mathbb E[(h(x)-m(x))(h(y)-m(y))]. $$ The expectation runs over possible maps, or over cells assumed to share these statistics. These two functions determine every finite joint distribution. A Gaussian process can thus produce many different curves while keeping a precise rule for their spatial dependence. [A [**jointly Gaussian vector**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is one for which every linear combination of its entries is Gaussian.]{.definition-explanation} For this family, zero covariance between two subvectors implies their independence. That extra property, which does not hold for general distributions, will simplify the crossing calculation. The values after thresholding will generally not have a Gaussian distribution.[^p3-model] ::: Three assumptions have different jobs: - [[**Stationarity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that moving the observation window does not change the map's probability law. Here it gives a constant mean and a covariance $C(x,y)=C(y-x)$ that depends on separation.]{.definition-explanation} It does not say that a particular map is flat. - [[**Isotropy**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that rotating the separation does not change the covariance: in several dimensions, $C(\Delta x)$ depends only on $\|\Delta x\|$.]{.definition-explanation} It rules out a preferred direction in the model's statistics. Stationarity alone does not imply isotropy. - [[**Smoothness**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} controls whether the map has well defined spatial derivatives.]{.definition-explanation} Crossing calculations require differentiable sample functions and nondegenerate joint distributions: the relevant vector of heights and derivatives must have an invertible covariance matrix, rather than obey an exact linear constraint. Peak calculations require second derivatives and enough regularity to control their local approximation. A Gaussian distribution of values does not guarantee this smoothness. For example, a covariance proportional to $e^{-|x-y|/b}$ has a sharp corner at zero separation and does not supply the differentiable paths assumed below. Set the mean to zero and write $\sigma_h^2=C(0)$ for input variance. A constant input mean can be absorbed into the threshold. It is useful to normalize the input, $$ z(x)=\frac{h(x)}{\sigma_h},\qquad F(x)=a\,[z(x)-q]_+, \quad [u]_+=\max(u,0). $$ Here $z$ has variance one, $q$ is a dimensionless threshold, and $a>0$ converts normalized input to firing rate, in Hz. The paper writes $\theta$ for $q$, $r$ for covariance, and $D$ for spatial dimension; this guide uses $q,C,d$ to avoid conflicts with earlier chapters. The original input threshold is $q\sigma_h$. In the paper's Equation 3 the firing rate is proportional to $[h-q\sigma_h]_+$, which is equivalent to this form after choosing the gain.[^p3-model] The input threshold summarizes how much combined input is needed before the model cell fires. It can reflect the cell's own response properties and inhibitory input. Raising $q$ at a fixed input map leaves fewer positions active. If the absolute threshold above the input mean is positive and held fixed, increasing the input standard deviation $\sigma_h$ lowers $q$, making activity more widespread. Changing $a$ instead changes rates within active regions while preserving their zero-rate boundaries. A fixed positive detection cutoff in Hz would change this last conclusion. [A fitted threshold describes the balance of input and response; it does not identify which biological quantity changed.]{.key-statement}
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 1
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-1}}
[The [**excursion set**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} above $q$ is]{.definition-explanation} $$ A_q=\{x:z(x)>q\}. $$ Each connected piece of $A_q$ is a model place field. In one dimension its size is length. In two and three dimensions it is area and volume. [Two nearby peaks belong to one field if an above-threshold path joins them. Smoothness and stationarity alone do not ensure this independence.]{.key-statement} A periodic Gaussian process, for example, retains long distance dependence. Upward and downward crossings that enclose the same small field remain strongly related even when fields far apart are almost independent. Experimental selection also matters. If cells with no fields are excluded, a Poisson model with unconditioned mean $\lambda$ gives $$ \Pr(N=n\mid N\ge1)= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n}{n!(1-e^{-\lambda})},\quad n\ge1, \qquad \mathbb E[N\mid N\ge1]=\frac{\lambda}{1-e^{-\lambda}}. $$ The mean follows because the omitted $n=0$ term contributes zero to $\sum n\Pr(N=n)=\lambda$, while conditioning divides all remaining probabilities by $1-e^{-\lambda}$. For $\lambda=1$, $36.8\%$ of cells are excluded and the observed mean is $1.582$, not one. Using $1.582$ as the unconditioned mean would infer too many fields. The paper applies this correction to its two dimensional count fit, Equation 5.[^p3-selection] [^p3-question]: Mainali, N., Azeredo da Silveira, R., & Burak, Y. "At a uniformly chosen position, the probability of activity is $Q(q)$."
"Hence a track of length $L$ has expected occupied length $LQ(q)$."
"On a long stationary track, the average occupied length per field is the occupied length per unit distance divided by the number of fields per unit distance."
"The corresponding gap calculation uses the inactive fraction $\Phi(q)$:"
"$$ \begin{aligned} \mu_s&=\frac{Q(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma Q(q)e^{q^2/2},\\ \mu_g&=\frac{\Phi(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma\Phi(q)e^{q^2/2}. \end{aligned} $$"
"Subject to suitable averaging over a long track or many maps, they give the inference rule in Methods S3, Equations S14–S15.[^p3-means]"
"These are stationary per-field and per-gap means, ignoring clipping at track boundaries."
"They are not an assertion that the expectation of a finite sample's ratio equals the ratio of its expectations."
"Adding and dividing removes one unknown at a time:"
"$$ \mu_s+\mu_g=2\pi\sigma e^{q^2/2},\qquad \frac{\mu_s}{\mu_s+\mu_g}=Q(q). $$"
"Thus"
"$$ q=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\mu_g}{\mu_s+\mu_g}\right), \qquad \sigma=\frac{\mu_s+\mu_g}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2}. $$"

"For example, $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m, the fitted parameters reported for the 200 m bat tunnel, give $Q(q)=0.1357$, $\nu_+=0.03621$ per metre, $\mu_s=3.746$ m, and $\mu_g=23.868$ m in the continuous model."
"Putting these two means into the inversion recovers $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m."
"The expected number of intersecting fields on a 200 m track is $7.2425+0.1357=7.3782$, including the left endpoint term."
"These are calculations from the fitted model, not fresh estimates from raw recordings."

paragraphs.text: [Knowing the average field length does not tell us how often very small or very large fields occur. Why should the same spatial model give one size distribution on a track, another in an arena, and a third in a room?]{.key-statement} The next step is to find the shape of a typical field when only unusually high input peaks rise above the threshold.

Near such a peak, the smooth input is approximately a downward parabola. Its height above the threshold sets a radius, and converting that radius into length, area or volume gives the different size laws. Cuts through a map test its spatial structure, and slopes at field edges provide a separate check on the predicted field widths. [The size laws use a high threshold approximation; the boundary-slope law has a separate exact derivation under the smooth stationary Gaussian assumptions.]{.key-statement}

We keep the earlier notation: $z(x)$ is the spatial input normalized to variance one, $q$ is its threshold, $\sigma$ is its local distance scale, and $a$ converts positive excess input into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is $d$. The firing rule remains $F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+$, where $[u]_+=\max(u,0)$.

review_metadata.title: High peaks explain size laws across dimensions
review_metadata.purpose: A place cell’s active regions can have different sizes on a route, across a floor, or in a flight volume. This chapter derives why the spatial model predicts different field-size distributions in one, two, and three dimensions, and identifies the high-threshold approximation used in that derivation.

section_list.title: Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolic
section_list.summary: The crossing calculation determines a mean length exactly, but it does not yet explain the shape of the length histogram. To obtain that distribution, we examine the small region around a peak that barely exceeds a high threshold.

section_list.title: Geometry gives different size laws in each dimension
section_list.summary: A round region's radius and its volume have different units and different distributions. This geometric conversion explains why the model predicts different histograms in a track, an arena, and a room.

section_list.title: Slices test spatial structure beyond field volume
section_list.summary: A model can fit field volumes and still place activity incorrectly within those volumes. Slicing the map tests that internal spatial structure.

section_list.title: Why slopes at field boundaries are Rayleigh
section_list.summary: The derivative at an arbitrary position is Gaussian. A field boundary is a selected position, however, and selecting it changes the derivative distribution.

# High peaks explain size laws across dimensions {#ch:PLACE-SIZES} [Knowing the average field length does not tell us how often very small or very large fields occur. Why should the same spatial model give one size distribution on a track, another in an arena, and a third in a room?]{.key-statement} The next step is to find the shape of a typical field when only unusually high input peaks rise above the threshold. Near such a peak, the smooth input is approximately a downward parabola. Its height above the threshold sets a radius, and converting that radius into length, area or volume gives the different size laws. Cuts through a map test its spatial structure, and slopes at field edges provide a separate check on the predicted field widths. [The size laws use a high threshold approximation; the boundary-slope law has a separate exact derivation under the smooth stationary Gaussian assumptions.]{.key-statement} We keep the earlier notation: $z(x)$ is the spatial input normalized to variance one, $q$ is its threshold, $\sigma$ is its local distance scale, and $a$ converts positive excess input into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is $d$. The firing rule remains $F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+$, where $[u]_+=\max(u,0)$. ## Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolic {#sec:PLACE-RARE-PEAKS} The crossing calculation determines a mean length exactly, but it does not yet explain the shape of the length histogram. To obtain that distribution, we examine the small region around a peak that barely exceeds a high threshold. The following is a teaching reconstruction of the high excursion argument in Methods S4, with algebraic corrections made explicit below. It assumes: - a sufficiently smooth, stationary, isotropic, unit variance Gaussian field; - an invertible covariance matrix for the relevant derivative variables; - the limit $q\to\infty$; - typical components counted once each, away from environment boundaries. It is not a proof of the full excursion convergence theorem for every allowed covariance.[^p3-rare-source] [The [**Hessian**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the matrix $H$ of second spatial derivatives; its eigenvalues describe curvature along the principal directions.]{.definition-explanation} Isotropy and the definition of $\sigma$ imply $$ \operatorname{Cov}(\partial_i\partial_j z,z) =-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\sigma^2}. $$ Here $\delta_{ij}$ is one for equal indices and zero otherwise. For jointly Gaussian variables, conditioning $Y$ on a scalar $Z$ of variance one gives $\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=b]=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)b$ when both means vanish. One way to see this is to write $Y=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)Z+\epsilon$; the remainder has zero covariance with $Z$ and is therefore independent of it. Applying this to each Hessian entry gives $$ \mathbb E[H\mid z=b]=-\frac{b}{\sigma^2}I. $$ The conditional fluctuations around this mean have a variance that does not grow with $b$. For a high peak, the negative mean curvature is of order $q$, so its relative fluctuations become small. Conditioning the gradient to zero does not change this Gaussian conditional mean, because the gradient has zero covariance with both height and Hessian in a stationary isotropic field. Selecting an actual maximum also weights curvatures, but its leading high peak shape is the same. Let the peak height be $q+\epsilon$, with $\epsilon>0$, and put the peak at the origin. The gradient there is zero. The Taylor expansion becomes, to leading order, $$ z(x)-q\simeq\epsilon-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}\|x\|^2. $$ It is positive inside an approximately round region of radius $$ r_*\simeq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon}{q}}. $$ The remaining question is how $\epsilon$ is distributed when we select one high field at a time. In one dimension, the number of high maxima is asymptotically the number of upcrossings, proportional to $e^{-q^2/2}$. Therefore the fraction of peaks above $q$ that also exceed $q+\epsilon$ is approximately $$ \frac{e^{-(q+\epsilon)^2/2}}{e^{-q^2/2}} =e^{-q\epsilon-\epsilon^2/2}. $$ Define $U=q\epsilon$. At fixed $u\ge0$ and as $q$ increases, $$ \Pr(U>u)\simeq e^{-u-u^2/(2q^2)}\longrightarrow e^{-u}. $$ [Thus the scaled excess height approaches an exponential variable of mean one.]{.key-statement} In several dimensions, high peak counts have the additional leading factor $q^{d-1}$. Its ratio at $q+u/q$ and $q$ tends to one, so the same excess-height limit remains. The higher dimensional count factor will also follow from the [Euler characteristic calculation](ch-place-tests.html#sec-place-topology). A rigorous conclusion requires control of the remainder and of components containing multiple peaks, beyond this local argument. In one dimension, the full field length is $s=2r_*$. Eliminating $\epsilon$ gives $$ s\simeq\frac{2\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\sqrt U, \qquad \epsilon\simeq\frac{q s^2}{8\sigma^2}. $$ This supplies two distinct predictions: - [The length is a scaled square root of an exponential variable, giving a [**Rayleigh distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} - The peak firing rate is $a\epsilon$, so at fixed high $q$ it is proportional to $s^2$. The exponent two concerns rate versus linear size. In three dimensions a suitable linear size is $s^{1/3}$ when $s$ denotes volume. At moderate thresholds the omitted shape fluctuations matter. Figure 3C reports a rate versus length exponent of $1.42$ in the 200 m bat data and $1.46$ in finite threshold model simulations. Figure 3D reports $1.75$ versus $1.71$ using cube root of volume in 3D. These are compatible with a model that approaches exponent two only as the threshold becomes large; they are not measurements of the limiting exponent. Figure 5A–C illustrates the progression toward simpler, usually single peak fields as $q$ increases. Figure 4C tests this trend in the shorter bat tunnel.[^p3-shapes]
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 5
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-5}}
## Geometry gives different size laws in each dimension {#sec:PLACE-SIZE-LAW} A round region's radius and its volume have different units and different distributions. This geometric conversion explains why the model predicts different histograms in a track, an arena, and a room. Let $v_d=\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(1+d/2)$ be the volume of a unit ball in $d$ dimensions. For $d=1,2,3$, it is $2,\pi,4\pi/3$. [The symbol $\Gamma$ is the [**gamma function**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, defined for $t>0$ by $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du$. It extends factorials: $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$.]{.definition-explanation} Using the radius from the preceding section, the field size is $$ s\simeq v_d\left(\frac{\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\right)^d U^{d/2}, \qquad U=\beta s^{2/d},\qquad \beta=\frac{q^2}{2\sigma^2v_d^{2/d}}. $$ The same local radius gives a length, an area, or a volume depending on the dimension of the region.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-GEOMETRY}}
The round shape and exponential excess belong to the high-threshold limit, so they do not make every measured place field spherical. Since the density of $U$ is $e^{-u}$ for $u>0$, changing variables gives $$ \begin{aligned} p_d(s)&=e^{-\beta s^{2/d}}\frac{d}{ds}(\beta s^{2/d})\\ &=\frac{2\beta}{d}s^{2/d-1}e^{-\beta s^{2/d}},\qquad s>0. \end{aligned} $$ This is the paper's Equation 1. The expression for $\beta$ above is its leading high threshold geometric scale, not an exact finite threshold identity. A finite threshold simulation can share the approximate shape while having a different fitted scale.[^p3-size-source] The mean and its corresponding scale are $$ \mu_s=\Gamma(1+d/2)\beta^{-d/2},\qquad \beta=\left[\frac{\Gamma(1+d/2)}{\mu_s}\right]^{2/d}. $$ ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: normalization and higher size moments"} Normalization needs no special integral: $\int_0^\infty p_d(s)\,ds=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du=1$. The same substitution supplies every positive moment, $$ \mathbb E[s^k] =\beta^{-kd/2}\int_0^\infty u^{kd/2}e^{-u}\,du =\beta^{-kd/2}\Gamma(1+kd/2). $$ ::: Size has units of distance to the power $d$, while $\beta$ has units of inverse distance squared in every dimension. This makes $\beta s^{2/d}$ dimensionless, and makes $p_d(s)$ a density per unit size. These checks catch mistakes in changing variables. Writing dimensionless size as $w=\beta^{d/2}s$ removes the size scale. The dimensional size laws then differ in shape, while the transformed variable $U=\beta s^{2/d}=w^{2/d}$ has the same exponential law.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-DENSITY-COLLAPSE}}
Removing units does not erase the difference between length, area, and volume distributions. The nonlinear transformation to U removes that shape difference; its shared exponential law is the assumption used in the change of variables. See [Field-size laws, Eq. 1, p. 1111](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=3).
{{block:tbl:PLACE-SIZE-LAWS}}
[A [**Weibull distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} has survival probability $\exp[-(s/b)^k]$ for size $s>0$, scale $b>0$, and shape $k>0$.]{.definition-explanation} Here $k=2/d$ and $b=\beta^{-d/2}$. In 3D the diverging density does not mean a positive probability of exactly zero volume; the probability of $0 Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 2
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-2}}
[The dashed analytical curves change with the dimension of the measurement, even within one recorded map. The alternative spherical-field model in Figure S2 matches empirical volumes and peak rates by construction but fails these slice distributions and the topology test. Matching volumes alone is therefore insufficient.]{.key-statement}[^p3-slices-source]
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure S2
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-S2}}
## Why slopes at field boundaries are Rayleigh {#sec:PLACE-SLOPES} The derivative at an arbitrary position is Gaussian. A field boundary is a selected position, however, and selecting it changes the derivative distribution. Return to the [crossing integral](ch-place-fields.html#sec-place-kac-rice) and retain only slopes between $v$ and $v+dv$. Their contribution is proportional to $v p_{z'}(v)dv$. Dividing by the total contribution of positive slopes gives the slope density at a typical upcrossing: $$ p_{\uparrow}(v) =\frac{v p_{z'}(v)}{\int_0^\infty w p_{z'}(w)\,dw} =\sigma^2v\exp[-\sigma^2v^2/2],\qquad v>0. $$ The height density cancels because height and slope are independent. [This Rayleigh law is therefore independent of $q$ under the smooth stationary Gaussian model, without a high threshold approximation.]{.key-statement} Absolute slopes at downward boundaries have the same law. The rate slope is $av$, so its scale also depends on the firing rate gain. This selection effect explains why a half Gaussian law for a positive derivative sampled uniformly in space would be wrong at crossings.[^p3-slope-source] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Independent check: recover field width from its boundary slope"} There is also an independent check on the high threshold width constant. Starting at an upcrossing with slope $v$, the local excursion is approximately $$ z(x)-q\simeq vx-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}x^2. $$ Its second root is $s=2\sigma^2v/q$. Changing variables in the exact crossing slope law gives $p(s)=2\beta s e^{-\beta s^2}$ with $\beta=q^2/(8\sigma^2)$, the same constant as the peak calculation for $v_1=2$. ::: Figure 3A identifies which width, peak, and slopes are measured. B compares local peak counts, C–D compare rate and size, and E compares boundary slopes. The paper measures boundary slopes by a finite difference between samples 0.1 m apart. This approximates a derivative and has its own spatial resolution. It is not a direct observation of the underlying synaptic input.
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 3
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-3}}

## Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolic {#sec:PLACE-RARE-PEAKS} The crossing calculation determines a mean length exactly, but it does not yet explain the shape of the length histogram. To obtain that distribution, we examine the small region around a peak that barely exceeds a high threshold. The following is a teaching reconstruction of the high excursion argument in Methods S4, with algebraic corrections made explicit below. It assumes: - a sufficiently smooth, stationary, isotropic, unit variance Gaussian field; - an invertible covariance matrix for the relevant derivative variables; - the limit $q\to\infty$; - typical components counted once each, away from environment boundaries. It is not a proof of the full excursion convergence theorem for every allowed covariance.[^p3-rare-source] [The [**Hessian**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the matrix $H$ of second spatial derivatives; its eigenvalues describe curvature along the principal directions.]{.definition-explanation} Isotropy and the definition of $\sigma$ imply $$ \operatorname{Cov}(\partial_i\partial_j z,z) =-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\sigma^2}. $$ Here $\delta_{ij}$ is one for equal indices and zero otherwise. For jointly Gaussian variables, conditioning $Y$ on a scalar $Z$ of variance one gives $\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=b]=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)b$ when both means vanish. One way to see this is to write $Y=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)Z+\epsilon$; the remainder has zero covariance with $Z$ and is therefore independent of it. Applying this to each Hessian entry gives $$ \mathbb E[H\mid z=b]=-\frac{b}{\sigma^2}I. $$ The conditional fluctuations around this mean have a variance that does not grow with $b$. For a high peak, the negative mean curvature is of order $q$, so its relative fluctuations become small. Conditioning the gradient to zero does not change this Gaussian conditional mean, because the gradient has zero covariance with both height and Hessian in a stationary isotropic field. Selecting an actual maximum also weights curvatures, but its leading high peak shape is the same. Let the peak height be $q+\epsilon$, with $\epsilon>0$, and put the peak at the origin. The gradient there is zero. The Taylor expansion becomes, to leading order, $$ z(x)-q\simeq\epsilon-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}\|x\|^2. $$ It is positive inside an approximately round region of radius $$ r_*\simeq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon}{q}}. $$ The remaining question is how $\epsilon$ is distributed when we select one high field at a time. In one dimension, the number of high maxima is asymptotically the number of upcrossings, proportional to $e^{-q^2/2}$. Therefore the fraction of peaks above $q$ that also exceed $q+\epsilon$ is approximately $$ \frac{e^{-(q+\epsilon)^2/2}}{e^{-q^2/2}} =e^{-q\epsilon-\epsilon^2/2}. $$ Define $U=q\epsilon$. At fixed $u\ge0$ and as $q$ increases, $$ \Pr(U>u)\simeq e^{-u-u^2/(2q^2)}\longrightarrow e^{-u}. $$ [Thus the scaled excess height approaches an exponential variable of mean one.]{.key-statement} In several dimensions, high peak counts have the additional leading factor $q^{d-1}$. Its ratio at $q+u/q$ and $q$ tends to one, so the same excess-height limit remains. The higher dimensional count factor will also follow from the [Euler characteristic calculation](ch-place-tests.html#sec-place-topology). A rigorous conclusion requires control of the remainder and of components containing multiple peaks, beyond this local argument. In one dimension, the full field length is $s=2r_*$. Eliminating $\epsilon$ gives $$ s\simeq\frac{2\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\sqrt U, \qquad \epsilon\simeq\frac{q s^2}{8\sigma^2}. $$ This supplies two distinct predictions: - [The length is a scaled square root of an exponential variable, giving a [**Rayleigh distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} - The peak firing rate is $a\epsilon$, so at fixed high $q$ it is proportional to $s^2$. The exponent two concerns rate versus linear size. In three dimensions a suitable linear size is $s^{1/3}$ when $s$ denotes volume. At moderate thresholds the omitted shape fluctuations matter. Figure 3C reports a rate versus length exponent of $1.42$ in the 200 m bat data and $1.46$ in finite threshold model simulations. Figure 3D reports $1.75$ versus $1.71$ using cube root of volume in 3D. These are compatible with a model that approaches exponent two only as the threshold becomes large; they are not measurements of the limiting exponent. Figure 5A–C illustrates the progression toward simpler, usually single peak fields as $q$ increases. Figure 4C tests this trend in the shorter bat tunnel.[^p3-shapes]
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 5

review_metadata.title: High peaks explain size laws across dimensions
review_metadata.purpose: A place cell’s active regions can have different sizes on a route, across a floor, or in a flight volume. This chapter derives why the spatial model predicts different field-size distributions in one, two, and three dimensions, and identifies the high-threshold approximation used in that derivation.

section_list.title: Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolic
section_list.summary: The crossing calculation determines a mean length exactly, but it does not yet explain the shape of the length histogram. To obtain that distribution, we examine the small region around a peak that barely exceeds a high threshold.

section_list.title: Geometry gives different size laws in each dimension
section_list.summary: A round region's radius and its volume have different units and different distributions. This geometric conversion explains why the model predicts different histograms in a track, an arena, and a room.

section_list.title: Slices test spatial structure beyond field volume
section_list.summary: A model can fit field volumes and still place activity incorrectly within those volumes. Slicing the map tests that internal spatial structure.

section_list.title: Why slopes at field boundaries are Rayleigh
section_list.summary: The derivative at an arbitrary position is Gaussian. A field boundary is a selected position, however, and selecting it changes the derivative distribution.

# High peaks explain size laws across dimensions {#ch:PLACE-SIZES} [Knowing the average field length does not tell us how often very small or very large fields occur. Why should the same spatial model give one size distribution on a track, another in an arena, and a third in a room?]{.key-statement} The next step is to find the shape of a typical field when only unusually high input peaks rise above the threshold. Near such a peak, the smooth input is approximately a downward parabola. Its height above the threshold sets a radius, and converting that radius into length, area or volume gives the different size laws. Cuts through a map test its spatial structure, and slopes at field edges provide a separate check on the predicted field widths. [The size laws use a high threshold approximation; the boundary-slope law has a separate exact derivation under the smooth stationary Gaussian assumptions.]{.key-statement} We keep the earlier notation: $z(x)$ is the spatial input normalized to variance one, $q$ is its threshold, $\sigma$ is its local distance scale, and $a$ converts positive excess input into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is $d$. The firing rule remains $F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+$, where $[u]_+=\max(u,0)$. ## Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolic {#sec:PLACE-RARE-PEAKS} The crossing calculation determines a mean length exactly, but it does not yet explain the shape of the length histogram. It is not a proof of the full excursion convergence theorem for every allowed covariance.[^p3-rare-source] [The [**Hessian**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the matrix $H$ of second spatial derivatives; its eigenvalues describe curvature along the principal directions.]{.definition-explanation} Isotropy and the definition of $\sigma$ imply $$ \operatorname{Cov}(\partial_i\partial_j z,z) =-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\sigma^2}. $$ Here $\delta_{ij}$ is one for equal indices and zero otherwise. For jointly Gaussian variables, conditioning $Y$ on a scalar $Z$ of variance one gives $\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=b]=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)b$ when both means vanish. One way to see this is to write $Y=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)Z+\epsilon$; the remainder has zero covariance with $Z$ and is therefore independent of it. Applying this to each Hessian entry gives $$ \mathbb E[H\mid z=b]=-\frac{b}{\sigma^2}I. $$ The conditional fluctuations around this mean have a variance that does not grow with $b$. For a high peak, the negative mean curvature is of order $q$, so its relative fluctuations become small. Conditioning the gradient to zero does not change this Gaussian conditional mean, because the gradient has zero covariance with both height and Hessian in a stationary isotropic field. Selecting an actual maximum also weights curvatures, but its leading high peak shape is the same. Let the peak height be $q+\epsilon$, with $\epsilon>0$, and put the peak at the origin. The gradient there is zero. The Taylor expansion becomes, to leading order, $$ z(x)-q\simeq\epsilon-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}\|x\|^2. $$ It is positive inside an approximately round region of radius $$ r_*\simeq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon}{q}}. $$ The remaining question is how $\epsilon$ is distributed when we select one high field at a time. In one dimension, the number of high maxima is asymptotically the number of upcrossings, proportional to $e^{-q^2/2}$. Therefore the fraction of peaks above $q$ that also exceed $q+\epsilon$ is approximately $$ \frac{e^{-(q+\epsilon)^2/2}}{e^{-q^2/2}} =e^{-q\epsilon-\epsilon^2/2}. $$ Define $U=q\epsilon$. ## Geometry gives different size laws in each dimension {#sec:PLACE-SIZE-LAW} A round region's radius and its volume have different units and different distributions. This geometric conversion explains why the model predicts different histograms in a track, an arena, and a room. Let $v_d=\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(1+d/2)$ be the volume of a unit ball in $d$ dimensions. For $d=1,2,3$, it is $2,\pi,4\pi/3$. [The symbol $\Gamma$ is the [**gamma function**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, defined for $t>0$ by $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du$. It extends factorials: $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$.]{.definition-explanation} Using the radius from the preceding section, the field size is $$ s\simeq v_d\left(\frac{\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\right)^d U^{d/2}, \qquad U=\beta s^{2/d},\qquad \beta=\frac{q^2}{2\sigma^2v_d^{2/d}}. $$ The same local radius gives a length, an area, or a volume depending on the dimension of the region.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-GEOMETRY}}
The round shape and exponential excess belong to the high-threshold limit, so they do not make every measured place field spherical. Since the density of $U$ is $e^{-u}$ for $u>0$, changing variables gives $$ \begin{aligned} p_d(s)&=e^{-\beta s^{2/d}}\frac{d}{ds}(\beta s^{2/d})\\ &=\frac{2\beta}{d}s^{2/d-1}e^{-\beta s^{2/d}},\qquad s>0. \end{aligned} $$ This is the paper's Equation 1. The expression for $\beta$ above is its leading high threshold geometric scale, not an exact finite threshold identity. A finite threshold simulation can share the approximate shape while having a different fitted scale.[^p3-size-source] The mean and its corresponding scale are $$ \mu_s=\Gamma(1+d/2)\beta^{-d/2},\qquad \beta=\left[\frac{\Gamma(1+d/2)}{\mu_s}\right]^{2/d}. $$ ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: normalization and higher size moments"} Normalization needs no special integral: $\int_0^\infty p_d(s)\,ds=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du=1$. The same substitution supplies every positive moment, $$ \mathbb E[s^k] =\beta^{-kd/2}\int_0^\infty u^{kd/2}e^{-u}\,du =\beta^{-kd/2}\Gamma(1+kd/2). $$ ::: Size has units of distance to the power $d$, while $\beta$ has units of inverse distance squared in every dimension. This makes $\beta s^{2/d}$ dimensionless, and makes $p_d(s)$ a density per unit size. These checks catch mistakes in changing variables. Writing dimensionless size as $w=\beta^{d/2}s$ removes the size scale. The dimensional size laws then differ in shape, while the transformed variable $U=\beta s^{2/d}=w^{2/d}$ has the same exponential law.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-DENSITY-COLLAPSE}}
Removing units does not erase the difference between length, area, and volume distributions. The nonlinear transformation to U removes that shape difference; its shared exponential law is the assumption used in the change of variables. See [Field-size laws, Eq. 1, p. 1111](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=3).
{{block:tbl:PLACE-SIZE-LAWS}}
[A [**Weibull distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} has survival probability $\exp[-(s/b)^k]$ for size $s>0$, scale $b>0$, and shape $k>0$.]{.definition-explanation} Here $k=2/d$ and $b=\beta^{-d/2}$. In 3D the diverging density does not mean a positive probability of exactly zero volume; the probability of $0 Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 2
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-2}}
[The dashed analytical curves change with the dimension of the measurement, even within one recorded map. The alternative spherical-field model in Figure S2 matches empirical volumes and peak rates by construction but fails these slice distributions and the topology test. Matching volumes alone is therefore insufficient.]{.key-statement}[^p3-slices-source]
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure S2
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-S2}}
## Why slopes at field boundaries are Rayleigh {#sec:PLACE-SLOPES} The derivative at an arbitrary position is Gaussian. A field boundary is a selected position, however, and selecting it changes the derivative distribution. Return to the [crossing integral](ch-place-fields.html#sec-place-kac-rice) and retain only slopes between $v$ and $v+dv$. Their contribution is proportional to $v p_{z'}(v)dv$. Dividing by the total contribution of positive slopes gives the slope density at a typical upcrossing: $$ p_{\uparrow}(v) =\frac{v p_{z'}(v)}{\int_0^\infty w p_{z'}(w)\,dw} =\sigma^2v\exp[-\sigma^2v^2/2],\qquad v>0. $$ The height density cancels because height and slope are independent. [This Rayleigh law is therefore independent of $q$ under the smooth stationary Gaussian model, without a high threshold approximation.]{.key-statement} Absolute slopes at downward boundaries have the same law. The rate slope is $av$, so its scale also depends on the firing rate gain. This selection effect explains why a half Gaussian law for a positive derivative sampled uniformly in space would be wrong at crossings.[^p3-slope-source] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Independent check: recover field width from its boundary slope"} There is also an independent check on the high threshold width constant. Starting at an upcrossing with slope $v$, the local excursion is approximately $$ z(x)-q\simeq vx-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}x^2. $$ Its second root is $s=2\sigma^2v/q$. Changing variables in the exact crossing slope law gives $p(s)=2\beta s e^{-\beta s^2}$ with $\beta=q^2/(8\sigma^2)$, the same constant as the peak calculation for $v_1=2$. ::: Figure 3A identifies which width, peak, and slopes are measured. B compares local peak counts, C–D compare rate and size, and E compares boundary slopes. The paper measures boundary slopes by a finite difference between samples 0.1 m apart. This approximates a derivative and has its own spatial resolution. It is not a direct observation of the underlying synaptic input.

Size has units of distance to the power $d$, while $\beta$ has units of inverse distance squared in every dimension. This makes $\beta s^{2/d}$ dimensionless, and makes $p_d(s)$ a density per unit size. These checks catch mistakes in changing variables.

Writing dimensionless size as $w=\beta^{d/2}s$ removes the size scale. The dimensional size laws then differ in shape, while the transformed variable $U=\beta s^{2/d}=w^{2/d}$ has the same exponential law.
<div class="figure-scroll">

<div class="table-responsive">

[A [**Weibull distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} has survival probability $\exp[-(s/b)^k]$ for size $s>0$, scale $b>0$, and shape $k>0$.]{.definition-explanation} Here $k=2/d$ and $b=\beta^{-d/2}$. In 3D the diverging density does not mean a positive probability of exactly zero volume; the probability of $0<s<\delta$ still tends to zero as $\delta\to0$.

For a concrete comparison, set $\sigma=1$ m and $q=5$ in this limiting calculation. The mean size is $0.5013$ m in 1D, $0.2513$ m$^2$ in 2D, and $0.1260$ m$^3$ in 3D. These values describe the same local distance scale and threshold, rather than fields with the same numerical size in different units. More generally, the geometry and moment formula simplify to $\mu_s\simeq(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma/q)^d$.

This approximation has a measurable error even for a smooth Gaussian process. At $q=1.1,\sigma=2.4$ m, its 1D mean is $5.469$ m, compared with the [exact stationary crossing result](ch-place-fields.html#sec-place-inference) $3.746$ m, an overestimate of $46.0\%$. At $q=5$ the error is $3.73\%$. [This is why the paper compares data to finite threshold simulations as well as to limiting curves.]{.key-statement}
The printed supplement appears to contain three algebraic errors in this calculation:
Equation S18 prints multiplication by mean size where the preceding moment formula requires division.
Equation S23 omits a factor $\sqrt2$ when solving the parabola in S22 for full width.
In S25 the finite-height quadratic exponent should be negative.

The derivation above retains the main paper's distributional form and obtains the constants from the displayed parabola, the moment integral, and the independent crossing calculation. These corrections concern the printed derivation; they do not establish that the simulation code or empirical fits used the same mistakes.[^p3-corrections]

## Geometry gives different size laws in each dimension {#sec:PLACE-SIZE-LAW} A round region's radius and its volume have different units and different distributions. This geometric conversion explains why the model predicts different histograms in a track, an arena, and a room. Let $v_d=\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(1+d/2)$ be the volume of a unit ball in $d$ dimensions. For $d=1,2,3$, it is $2,\pi,4\pi/3$. [The symbol $\Gamma$ is the [**gamma function**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, defined for $t>0$ by $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du$. It extends factorials: $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$.]{.definition-explanation} Using the radius from the preceding section, the field size is $$ s\simeq v_d\left(\frac{\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\right)^d U^{d/2}, \qquad U=\beta s^{2/d},\qquad \beta=\frac{q^2}{2\sigma^2v_d^{2/d}}. $$ The same local radius gives a length, an area, or a volume depending on the dimension of the region.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-GEOMETRY}}
The round shape and exponential excess belong to the high-threshold limit, so they do not make every measured place field spherical. Since the density of $U$ is $e^{-u}$ for $u>0$, changing variables gives $$ \begin{aligned} p_d(s)&=e^{-\beta s^{2/d}}\frac{d}{ds}(\beta s^{2/d})\\ &=\frac{2\beta}{d}s^{2/d-1}e^{-\beta s^{2/d}},\qquad s>0. \end{aligned} $$ This is the paper's Equation 1. The expression for $\beta$ above is its leading high threshold geometric scale, not an exact finite threshold identity. A finite threshold simulation can share the approximate shape while having a different fitted scale.[^p3-size-source] The mean and its corresponding scale are $$ \mu_s=\Gamma(1+d/2)\beta^{-d/2},\qquad \beta=\left[\frac{\Gamma(1+d/2)}{\mu_s}\right]^{2/d}. $$ ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: normalization and higher size moments"} Normalization needs no special integral: $\int_0^\infty p_d(s)\,ds=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du=1$. The same substitution supplies every positive moment, $$ \mathbb E[s^k] =\beta^{-kd/2}\int_0^\infty u^{kd/2}e^{-u}\,du =\beta^{-kd/2}\Gamma(1+kd/2). $$ ::: Size has units of distance to the power $d$, while $\beta$ has units of inverse distance squared in every dimension. review_metadata.title: High peaks explain size laws across dimensions
review_metadata.purpose: A place cell’s active regions can have different sizes on a route, across a floor, or in a flight volume. This chapter derives why the spatial model predicts different field-size distributions in one, two, and three dimensions, and identifies the high-threshold approximation used in that derivation.

section_list.title: Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolic
section_list.summary: The crossing calculation determines a mean length exactly, but it does not yet explain the shape of the length histogram. To obtain that distribution, we examine the small region around a peak that barely exceeds a high threshold.

section_list.title: Geometry gives different size laws in each dimension
section_list.summary: A round region's radius and its volume have different units and different distributions. This geometric conversion explains why the model predicts different histograms in a track, an arena, and a room.

section_list.title: Slices test spatial structure beyond field volume
section_list.summary: A model can fit field volumes and still place activity incorrectly within those volumes. Slicing the map tests that internal spatial structure.

section_list.title: Why slopes at field boundaries are Rayleigh
section_list.summary: The derivative at an arbitrary position is Gaussian. A field boundary is a selected position, however, and selecting it changes the derivative distribution.

# High peaks explain size laws across dimensions {#ch:PLACE-SIZES} [Knowing the average field length does not tell us how often very small or very large fields occur. Why should the same spatial model give one size distribution on a track, another in an arena, and a third in a room?]{.key-statement} The next step is to find the shape of a typical field when only unusually high input peaks rise above the threshold. Near such a peak, the smooth input is approximately a downward parabola. Its height above the threshold sets a radius, and converting that radius into length, area or volume gives the different size laws. Cuts through a map test its spatial structure, and slopes at field edges provide a separate check on the predicted field widths. [The size laws use a high threshold approximation; the boundary-slope law has a separate exact derivation under the smooth stationary Gaussian assumptions.]{.key-statement} We keep the earlier notation: $z(x)$ is the spatial input normalized to variance one, $q$ is its threshold, $\sigma$ is its local distance scale, and $a$ converts positive excess input into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is $d$. The firing rule remains $F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+$, where $[u]_+=\max(u,0)$. ## Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolic {#sec:PLACE-RARE-PEAKS} The crossing calculation determines a mean length exactly, but it does not yet explain the shape of the length histogram. To obtain that distribution, we examine the small region around a peak that barely exceeds a high threshold. The following is a teaching reconstruction of the high excursion argument in Methods S4, with algebraic corrections made explicit below. It assumes: - a sufficiently smooth, stationary, isotropic, unit variance Gaussian field; - an invertible covariance matrix for the relevant derivative variables; - the limit $q\to\infty$; - typical components counted once each, away from environment boundaries. It is not a proof of the full excursion convergence theorem for every allowed covariance.[^p3-rare-source] [The [**Hessian**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the matrix $H$ of second spatial derivatives; its eigenvalues describe curvature along the principal directions.]{.definition-explanation} Isotropy and the definition of $\sigma$ imply $$ \operatorname{Cov}(\partial_i\partial_j z,z) =-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\sigma^2}. $$ Here $\delta_{ij}$ is one for equal indices and zero otherwise. For jointly Gaussian variables, conditioning $Y$ on a scalar $Z$ of variance one gives $\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=b]=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)b$ when both means vanish. One way to see this is to write $Y=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)Z+\epsilon$; the remainder has zero covariance with $Z$ and is therefore independent of it. Applying this to each Hessian entry gives $$ \mathbb E[H\mid z=b]=-\frac{b}{\sigma^2}I. $$ The conditional fluctuations around this mean have a variance that does not grow with $b$. For a high peak, the negative mean curvature is of order $q$, so its relative fluctuations become small. Conditioning the gradient to zero does not change this Gaussian conditional mean, because the gradient has zero covariance with both height and Hessian in a stationary isotropic field. Selecting an actual maximum also weights curvatures, but its leading high peak shape is the same. Let the peak height be $q+\epsilon$, with $\epsilon>0$, and put the peak at the origin. The gradient there is zero. The Taylor expansion becomes, to leading order, $$ z(x)-q\simeq\epsilon-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}\|x\|^2. $$ It is positive inside an approximately round region of radius $$ r_*\simeq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon}{q}}. $$ The remaining question is how $\epsilon$ is distributed when we select one high field at a time. In one dimension, the number of high maxima is asymptotically the number of upcrossings, proportional to $e^{-q^2/2}$. Therefore the fraction of peaks above $q$ that also exceed $q+\epsilon$ is approximately $$ \frac{e^{-(q+\epsilon)^2/2}}{e^{-q^2/2}} =e^{-q\epsilon-\epsilon^2/2}. $$ Define $U=q\epsilon$. At fixed $u\ge0$ and as $q$ increases, $$ \Pr(U>u)\simeq e^{-u-u^2/(2q^2)}\longrightarrow e^{-u}. $$ [Thus the scaled excess height approaches an exponential variable of mean one.]{.key-statement} In several dimensions, high peak counts have the additional leading factor $q^{d-1}$. Its ratio at $q+u/q$ and $q$ tends to one, so the same excess-height limit remains. The higher dimensional count factor will also follow from the [Euler characteristic calculation](ch-place-tests.html#sec-place-topology). A rigorous conclusion requires control of the remainder and of components containing multiple peaks, beyond this local argument. In one dimension, the full field length is $s=2r_*$. Eliminating $\epsilon$ gives $$ s\simeq\frac{2\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\sqrt U, \qquad \epsilon\simeq\frac{q s^2}{8\sigma^2}. $$ This supplies two distinct predictions: - [The length is a scaled square root of an exponential variable, giving a [**Rayleigh distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} - The peak firing rate is $a\epsilon$, so at fixed high $q$ it is proportional to $s^2$. The exponent two concerns rate versus linear size. In three dimensions a suitable linear size is $s^{1/3}$ when $s$ denotes volume. At moderate thresholds the omitted shape fluctuations matter. Figure 3C reports a rate versus length exponent of $1.42$ in the 200 m bat data and $1.46$ in finite threshold model simulations. Figure 3D reports $1.75$ versus $1.71$ using cube root of volume in 3D. These are compatible with a model that approaches exponent two only as the threshold becomes large; they are not measurements of the limiting exponent. Figure 5A–C illustrates the progression toward simpler, usually single peak fields as $q$ increases. Figure 4C tests this trend in the shorter bat tunnel.[^p3-shapes]

[The symbol $\Gamma$ is the [**gamma function**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, defined for $t>0$ by $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du$. It extends factorials: $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$.]{.definition-explanation} Using the radius from the preceding section, the field size is $$ s\simeq v_d\left(\frac{\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\right)^d U^{d/2}, \qquad U=\beta s^{2/d},\qquad \beta=\frac{q^2}{2\sigma^2v_d^{2/d}}. $$ The same local radius gives a length, an area, or a volume depending on the dimension of the region.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-GEOMETRY}}
The round shape and exponential excess belong to the high-threshold limit, so they do not make every measured place field spherical. Since the density of $U$ is $e^{-u}$ for $u>0$, changing variables gives $$ \begin{aligned} p_d(s)&=e^{-\beta s^{2/d}}\frac{d}{ds}(\beta s^{2/d})\\ &=\frac{2\beta}{d}s^{2/d-1}e^{-\beta s^{2/d}},\qquad s>0. \end{aligned} $$ This is the paper's Equation 1. The expression for $\beta$ above is its leading high threshold geometric scale, not an exact finite threshold identity. A finite threshold simulation can share the approximate shape while having a different fitted scale.[^p3-size-source] The mean and its corresponding scale are $$ \mu_s=\Gamma(1+d/2)\beta^{-d/2},\qquad \beta=\left[\frac{\Gamma(1+d/2)}{\mu_s}\right]^{2/d}. $$ ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: normalization and higher size moments"} Normalization needs no special integral: $\int_0^\infty p_d(s)\,ds=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du=1$. The same substitution supplies every positive moment, $$ \mathbb E[s^k] =\beta^{-kd/2}\int_0^\infty u^{kd/2}e^{-u}\,du =\beta^{-kd/2}\Gamma(1+kd/2). $$ ::: Size has units of distance to the power $d$, while $\beta$ has units of inverse distance squared in every dimension. This makes $\beta s^{2/d}$ dimensionless, and makes $p_d(s)$ a density per unit size. These checks catch mistakes in changing variables. Writing dimensionless size as $w=\beta^{d/2}s$ removes the size scale. The dimensional size laws then differ in shape, while the transformed variable $U=\beta s^{2/d}=w^{2/d}$ has the same exponential law.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-DENSITY-COLLAPSE}}
Removing units does not erase the difference between length, area, and volume distributions. The nonlinear transformation to U removes that shape difference; its shared exponential law is the assumption used in the change of variables. See [Field-size laws, Eq. 1, p. 1111](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=3).
{{block:tbl:PLACE-SIZE-LAWS}}
[A [**Weibull distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} has survival probability $\exp[-(s/b)^k]$ for size $s>0$, scale $b>0$, and shape $k>0$.]{.definition-explanation} Here $k=2/d$ and $b=\beta^{-d/2}$. In 3D the diverging density does not mean a positive probability of exactly zero volume; the probability of $0 Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 2
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-2}}
[The dashed analytical curves change with the dimension of the measurement, even within one recorded map. The alternative spherical-field model in Figure S2 matches empirical volumes and peak rates by construction but fails these slice distributions and the topology test. Matching volumes alone is therefore insufficient.]{.key-statement}[^p3-slices-source]
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure S2
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-S2}}
## Why slopes at field boundaries are Rayleigh {#sec:PLACE-SLOPES} The derivative at an arbitrary position is Gaussian. A field boundary is a selected position, however, and selecting it changes the derivative distribution. Return to the [crossing integral](ch-place-fields.html#sec-place-kac-rice) and retain only slopes between $v$ and $v+dv$. Their contribution is proportional to $v p_{z'}(v)dv$. Dividing by the total contribution of positive slopes gives the slope density at a typical upcrossing: $$ p_{\uparrow}(v) =\frac{v p_{z'}(v)}{\int_0^\infty w p_{z'}(w)\,dw} =\sigma^2v\exp[-\sigma^2v^2/2],\qquad v>0. $$ The height density cancels because height and slope are independent. [This Rayleigh law is therefore independent of $q$ under the smooth stationary Gaussian model, without a high threshold approximation.]{.key-statement} Absolute slopes at downward boundaries have the same law. The rate slope is $av$, so its scale also depends on the firing rate gain. This selection effect explains why a half Gaussian law for a positive derivative sampled uniformly in space would be wrong at crossings.[^p3-slope-source] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Independent check: recover field width from its boundary slope"} There is also an independent check on the high threshold width constant. Starting at an upcrossing with slope $v$, the local excursion is approximately $$ z(x)-q\simeq vx-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}x^2. $$ Its second root is $s=2\sigma^2v/q$. Changing variables in the exact crossing slope law gives $p(s)=2\beta s e^{-\beta s^2}$ with $\beta=q^2/(8\sigma^2)$, the same constant as the peak calculation for $v_1=2$. ::: Figure 3A identifies which width, peak, and slopes are measured. B compares local peak counts, C–D compare rate and size, and E compares boundary slopes. The paper measures boundary slopes by a finite difference between samples 0.1 m apart. This approximates a derivative and has its own spatial resolution. It is not a direct observation of the underlying synaptic input.
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 3
